MR. SPEAKER    STATEMENT ON QUESTION BY MEMBER FOR YUKON
speechtext:
While I am on my feet I may deal with the so-called question of privilege which was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Yukon.
Yesterday the hon. member for Yukon rose on a question of privilege respecting certain statements made by the Minister of Justice on Thursday, April 9. The question, he said, "is one which involves two separate factors, one concerning the translation from English to French, and second the translation from French to English as relayed by the translators in the translation booths". Following in the footsteps of the hon. member I will deal with this question first of all.
It is certainly inaccurate to use the words "translation" and "translators" in the present case. What we have in the house is rather "simultaneous interpretation" by "interpreters". The hon. member for Yukon adds that in this particular debate the translators did break down for a moment. One who understands the difficulties and niceties of both the English and French languages would surely realize that it is impossible to make a satisfactory simultaneous translation. The interpretation comes first; the translation follows, and is something else. Therefore only the text itself or the translation which appears the next day can be used exceptionally as a basis for a question of privilege, if such a question of privilege is at all admissible.
The hon. member, who is a student of parliamentary procedure, when he rose to speak yesterday had just heard a statement from the Chair to the effect that members should not raise so-called questions of privilege on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in the debates or the proceedings of the house, and that questions of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. When the hon. member objected to the use of the words "something that is false both in fact and in law" he must have known that the opinion I had just given was just as applicable to the use of those words by the Minister of Justice as it had been to the use of the same words by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. What I said then, which I can only repeat now, is that if the word "false" was applied to things said and not to an hon. member, the term ceases to be unparliamentary. Surely the hon. member does not expect me to revise my decision at this time.
I can only conclude that the allegations of the hon. member, in the circumstances in which they were made, that is after I had just ruled on the matter, do not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege but constitute an abuse of the rules of the house.

Since the statement I have prepared is of considerable length, and since I believe it would be valueless unless read, I ask permission to have it printed in Hansard.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to rise and bring my modest contribution to this debate in order to show that our country-and I sincerely believe this-is heading toward anarchy, because the present government, just like the previous one, does not seem to know where it is going exactly in matters of finance and economy.
Once again this year we have heard the Conservatives take the government severely to task for its deficits, and rightly so because, when they were sitting on this side, the Liberals did the same and what is more, during the last election campaign, they

The Budget-Mr. Belanger promised to balance the budget. They certainly pulled in a lot of votes that way, since many people believe we should live according to our means.
During the election campaign the Liberals also made much of the fact that they could solve that economic problem because they had within their ranks some very capable economists who would be able to find within the present financial system the necessary money to increase expenditures, to abolish the annual deficit, to pay the debt, all that without increasing taxes.
And the Conservatives, just like the Liberals when they were in the opposition, now blame the government for not increasing its expenditures for social welfare, for example, or for other purposes. In short, as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) so rightly said not long ago in a candid statement on T.V.: "There is no difference between Conservatives and Liberals."
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to find out the reason why people whom I believe to be intelligent, who certainly must have something remarkable, as they have been chosen by their fellow citizens to represent them in the national parliament, should act in the inconsistent way I mentioned a while ago, and change their minds, simply because they change sides in the house.
Why should those same people feel so capable of settling every problem when they are sitting in the opposition, but suddenly become paralysed when they come into power, and do exactly the opposite of what they promised the people during election time? To illustrate my point, I shall mention the budgetary deficit, the 11 per cent tax on building materials, the 1 per cent income tax increase, and the so-called disappearance of unemployment which became stagnant unemployment; we were promised a minister of agriculture for the east; but this too vanished from the program. We were also promised an increase of family allowances for every child, but this has been changed to school allowances for children between 16 and 18 years only; and I could mention many other promises.
The worst in this matter is that those mighty brains with such poor achievements, deride and brand as inefficient anybody who suggests new and bold solutions, without ever stopping to listen, consider and discuss their suggestions, or summing up the courage to refute them logically.
I have now come to the point where I believe that because they are led by their pride and arrogance, they become deaf and blind.

Mr. Speaker, it is precisely because I am conscious of the fact that it is illogical, under our present monetary system, to advocate an increase of expenditures without at the same time boosting taxes or adding to the national debt that before the government considers making heavier expenditures, I suggest once more that it carry out a monetary reform along the lines that we Social Crediters have been suggesting for several years.
To enable hon. members to better understand what I mean, I feel it is necessary to explain somewhat the present monetary system, not the one we advocate but the one Canada adheres to right now. Consequently, allow me to quote from a brochure which was published under the direction of the Conseil Economique Inc., whose president is none other than Mr. Eugene Therrien, Q.C., barrister, and of which Hon. Senator Vaillan-court is a director. Those two gentlemen can hardly be called Social Crediters.
The persons I have just mentioned allowed the publication of this pamphlet to induce French Canadians to favour the only two French Canadian banks in the country with their deposits and savings.
To obtain such results, they had to show what benefits they could offer in return, and you will be able to see for yourselves, in the light of some quotations from this booklet, that these persons confirm exactly what the Social Crediters have been saying for a long time, that is banks control money and credit in the country by the privilege they have to create credit and to destroy it.
Here is this small pamphlet entitled "Chartered banks and us". The pamphlet proceeds by questions and answers. The first question is as follows:
What is money?
If the Minister without Portfolio were here, I would ask him to give special attention to this question, because I remember that, during the last election on television, thousand dollar bills rained on his head so as to frighten people by the threat of inflation. The minister certainly did not understand the definition of the word money.
Here is the definition given in this pamphlet:
The public often imagines that money is essentially a bank-bill, but according to present habits of Canadians, the majority of monetary operations are done through cheques, or internal accounting operations in the banks (transfers from one client's account to another client's account). Currency, as a means of payment or exchange, may assume various forms:	metal currency, paper
currency, cheques etc as on the other hand, it
is called upon to play widely different roles in our national economy.

Further on, we find question number 4:
What is the banking system?
In paragraph 2, we read this:
But the Bank of Canada alone does not make up the banking system. Its role is only justified to the extent that the banks properly act as intermediaries between the Bank of Canada and the general public-
And here we find the names of the Banque Canadienne Nationale and the Banque Provinciate du Canada as illustrations.
The Canadian banking system, more particularly, provides for so-called "chartered" banks which we shall especially examine. Indeed, those banks play the most significant part in the monetary field, considering the place given in Canada to "scrip" money, that is money created by the chartered banks in their books.
Those banks, Mr. Speaker, are not afraid to frighten us by saying that chartered banks create money.
Under question 5:
Can it be said, then, that banks create money?
-we find the following answer:
Yes, indeed, the chartered banks do create money, but only so far as they have liquid assets available at the start.
And we are given a more concrete explanation by means of a diagram composed of five small squares connected to each other by arrows, with the explanation that $1,000 of savings in a chartered bank become $11,500, which means that they are multiplied by 11J, the amount then being made available to trade and industry.
That pamphlet was published to stimulate saving deposits by French Canadians in French Canadian banks to enable the latter also to multiply them by 11J in order to help our French Canadian business and industries.
Question no. 10 is as follows:
In what way does the bank give assistance?
Here is the answer:
The banker makes an "advance" (he opens a credit) to his customer. The operation, as far as bookkeeping is concerned, is very simple. Let us assume that bank's assets increase, for instance, by $10,000 and, the bank's liabilities, by $10,000. On the assets' side, next to this "extra amount", of $10,000 the following reference now appears: "advance made to Mr. X". On the liabilities' side, an account of $10,000 is open to Mr. X; from now on, he will be able to draw cheques to pay his suppliers, to settle his accounts with his workers, etc. His bank account has "been provided with funds".
Mr. X has no money, but he has a bank account.
Did the bank create money in that way?
Of course, this is a manner of speech. By opening a credit, the banker made $10,000 of new money available to his customer (in the books: bank money).
The Budget-Mr. Belanger
That is exactly what the banks are doing when they create money.
But if the bank may thus create money, why should it be interested in receiving our savings?
The answer is this:
Banks need only have a certain quantity of notes, only a certain amount of liquidity. Therefore, they may use the rest, if they observe the "legal reserves"-
-which is a compulsory 8 per cent reserve for chartered banks. The banks also decided themselves to provide another 7 per cent reserve, which means that on every deposit, the banks must set aside 15 per cent.
Now, if I apply the system explained in this pamphlet to an amount of $1,000 here is what will happen. If I deposit $1,000, 15 per cent of that amount, that is $150, will be set aside as a reserve. If you deduct that amount from the $1,000 the balance is $850, which, multiplied by 11J, as the banks are entitled to do, adds up to $9,775.
Now, that amount of $9,775 lent at 6 per cent yields $586.50. An average interest of 3 per cent is paid on savings, which represents $30. That leaves $536.50 and I shall be generous in taking off another 10 per cent for administration expenses, although that 10 per cent is usually charged to the borrower; however, 10 per cent of $9,775 gives $97.75. Therefore, for the $1,000 deposit, the banker will get $459 per year in interest.
It is precisely that privilege that Social Crediters would like to put an end, and they would like the government to take it over and keep it for the benefit of the Canadian nation.
It is because of that privilege that chartered banks control credit, and indirectly the governments and the economic life of all Canadian citizens. That is why we are asking the government to recover that power. Without such a reform, without taking back from the banks a privilege as dangerous and vexatious for the people as that one, the same unemployment crisis which is threatening the United States will also be at our door and it will be impossible for the government to guard against it.
That crisis I made reference to was the subject of an article published in Le Droit on March 24, 1964. Let me quote:
A report on the dangers of automation (Reuter agency, Washington).
A group of American professors, trade unionists and economists submitted to President Johnson a report where they point out the dangers of automation.
There is a danger that automation might give rise to "unprecendented economic and social disorders" in the United States, according to the 32 signatories of the report, among whom one notes Gunnar Yrdal, the economist of Swedish origin, and Nobel prize-winner Dr. Linus Pauling.

The Budget-Mr. Belanger The report states that the United States-and, some day, the rest of the world-will soon be at grips with a "revolution" which will see "an unlimited production by machinery with no need for the co-operation of human beings."
"Steps must therefore be taken to provide and income for everyone", added the authors of the report.
Mr. Speaker, one does not have to be an economist or even hold a university degree to understand that the monetary system of a country is the very basis of its economic and social life and that it is most difficult, if not impossible, to build something sound, good and lasting upon a faulty basis. We cannot, for instance, build a house on wobbly foundations. Well, that is exactly what we are trying to do, and we know the results, which can be summarized as follows: huge debts, a federal government in debt, shying away from provincial governments which also are in debt and which try to get the most out of the federal government, thus giving rise to frictions that are getting increasingly serious between the federal and provincial governments.
On the other hand, municipal governments also are in debt, the same as school boards, wherever they exist, and they in turn are looking more and more to the provincial governments for the financial assistance they need for their normal development, which again results in rather serious frictions. Then we come to the smallest but most important cell of society, the family. There again, we see that debts are causing rather serious frictions which sometimes result in broken homes.
And yet this country offers us the horrifying spectacle of stores and warehouses overflowing with goods of all kinds, while a whole army of unemployed are waiting in poverty for the opportunity to increase production even more. I think that situation, in our country, is very aptly described by this increasingly popular expression: the people of Canada are living in poverty in a land of plenty.
And at the rate things are going, in view of the observations I made a while ago in regard to automation, this is but a beginning.
I could go on for some time in the same vein describing the present economic position in this country as well as in many other countries where the same monetary system is in use.
The solution to the present problems-I will not venture to say the perfect solution as such a thing does not exist-rests in a monetary reform which would hand over to the government money and credit control.
I think it was a great prime minister of Great Britain, Disraeli, who once said:
Give me control over money and credit in any country and X do not care a rap about those who will be making legislation there.

Hon. Mackenzie King said, in one of his books:
It is useless for a government to speak of sovereignty if it has no control over its own money and credit.
Mr. Speaker, this proves, indeed, the importance of control over money and credit.
May I also quote some extracts of the encyclical Quadragesima Anno. Under the subtitle: "Domination has followed from free competition", we read:
In the first place, then, it is patent that in our days not alone is wealth accumulated, but immense power and despotic economic domination is concentrated in the hands of a few, and that those few are frequently not the owners, but only the trustees and directors of invested funds, who administer them at their good pleasure.
This power becomes particularly irresistible when exercised by those who, because they hold and control money, are able also to govern credit and determine its allotment, for that reason supplying, so to speak, the life blood of the entire economic body, and grasping, as it were, in their hands the very soul of production, so that no one dare breathe against their will.
And as for the consequences of such a system, this is what our Holy Father the Pope has to say:
Disastrous consequences-The whole economic life has become hard, cruel and relentless in a ghastly measure. Furthermore, the intermingling and scandalous confusion of the duties and offices of civil authority and of economics has produced crying evils and have gone so far as to degrade the majesty of the state. The state which should be the supreme arbiter, ruling in kingly fashion far above all party contention, intent only upon justice and the common good, has become instead a slave, bound over to the service of human passion and greed.
All this shows that we Social Crediters are not the only ones to deplore this serious deficiency in our country due to lack of control by the government over the most essential factor in our economy.
I think I have said enough to prove that the government, as well as the Canadian people, are the slaves of this system. Far from controlling it, they are controlled by it instead. That is why individuals, intelligent though they may be, are compelled to act in such a stupid way.
If the government would solve the financial problem along the lines I have just suggested, it could raise family allowances according to the present cost of living, improve the Old Age Assistance Act, the Old Age Security Act, as well as the Disabled Persons Act and the Blind Persons Act, so that when the husband falls under one or the other of those classifications and becomes eligible, to the assistance provided, the wife should also become eligible automatically. In addition, these pensions should be paid at 65, because I fail to see the purpose of keeping at work people over 60, 65 and 70 years of age while young people of 20, 30 or even 40 cannot

find work and might even go hungry. I am in favour of keeping at home the older people, but let us pay them a pension which will enable them to live decently, according to the standard of living which is possible in this country.
By agreeing to that monetary reform, the government would not have to constantly violate the constitution, to sacrifice the welfare of the people to the golden calf on the altar of finance, in short, to sacrifice confederation itself. In fact, we must not forget that this has been said and even proved following the last federal-provincial conference, for it is indeed financial matters which divide the provinces, Quebec especially, and the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that the problem of bilingualism, biculturalism, nationalism and racism is very important, but it behooves us also to settle financial problems which create so many difficulties.
I may seem to pay too much attention to social measures, but when you represent as I do a constituency where in wintertime, I would say at least half the families depend on social assistance, unemployment assistance or unemployment insurance benefits, you cannot help but find those social measures very important.
Along the same lines, I would ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to try and improve the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is very hard to understand and many zealous employees try by all possible means, by using the provisions of the act which they actually know much better than the recipients, to find a loop-hole that will prevent the unemployed from receiving his or her allowances. In brief, an act, or rather acts, were passed to help the unemployed and the underprivileged but, on the other hand, everything is done to prevent them from getting such help.
I would also like to remind the Minister of Labour that his intention, which he has just revealed, to place all school teachers in this country under the Unemployment Insurance Act is an unwholesome plan which will be met with much resistance. As far as I am concerned, I think it is an indirect, hypocritical and iniquitous way to tax people for something they will never take advantage of, for everyone knows that in the teaching profession, there is no unemployment and it will be a long time before there is.
I should also like to mention to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) that in my riding and in the neighbouring one there is a serious obstacle to trade and industrial development. It is the Saguenay river, which makes it necessary for all through traffic to use a ferry on which rates are very high, 20220-135
The Budget-Mr. Belanger almost prohibitive. In view of the alarming economic situation in that area, would it not be possible for the government to take the situation in hand and pay all ferry costs, which would be profitable for users and the whole population?
I will deal once more with highway No. 15, between Quebec city and Seven Islands, and suggest again that this government should come to an understanding with the provincial government, in order to make it a northern section of the trans-Canada highway. That would be one of the most urgent and most essential improvements if that region of Charlevoix and Saguenay is to develop at least as much as the other regions of Canada.
I also ask the government, as an emergency measure to fight acute unemployment in my riding, to build post offices which are so obviously needed, and to continue its policy of restoring and repairing the great number of wharves which need looking after.
I would like again this year to ask the government to make the necessary studies to find out definitely if the construction of a deep water wharf at Baie St. Paul is needed for and essential to the industrial and economic development of that region.
We are told that trade and industry in that region are not important enough to warrant the expense of building such a wharf. I feel that if the government were to make such an expenditure, its decision would be justified by the industrial and commercial development that would follow.
With the hon. member for St. John's West, I say that the primary objective of the government should be to fight poverty, want and hunger especially in Canada but also throughout the world. That would be possible through a monetary reform since all the means are at our disposal: the required production facilities, an abundance of products which more than satisfies Canada's needs and the necessary natural resources. That would be a much more efficient way of waging a cold war against communism than the sending of troops to the four corners of the globe.
I could not conclude without saying once more that it is imperative for the government to regain control of the money supply and credit and to take that privilege away from the banks.
It is to keep this privilege in favour of a small group of men that we are directed to have some works performed during the winter when it would be more appropriate and less costly to have them done in summer. It is on account of this privilege that the high cost of

The Budget-Mr. Rapp living is maintained, by forcing the public into paying twice or many times over for any single thing.
As an example, let us take the last world war, when the people provided the work, the materials and the soldiers; when it was all over, we owed $15 billion to those who had only written down the necessary figures to represent these expenditures. To keep this privilege, nobody even thought of stopping the war for lack of money, but today, families by the thousands are left in utter poverty because money is lacking. All this and many other things are stupid and would be ridiculous were they not criminal.
As long as the first and the most important concern of a nation consists in finding money, it will remain a slave, a materialist, and its morals will sink lower and lower.
Those are some of the reasons why I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and the government to implement as soon as possible the financial reforms which we have recommended. Unless he finds a better solution, a sad future lies ahead for his party and particularly for the Canadian people, and he will bear forever that heavy responsibility. You cannot keep the majority of the Canadian people in poverty for long without provoking violence when a high standard of living is physically possible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a good deal of pleasure to take part in the budget debate. It is a generally accepted rule that when a member takes part in this debate he should deal with matters pertaining to the budget, but I do not think it is an actual infringement of the rules if a member deals with other matters relating to the general business of the house, which it is my intention to do today.
The matters I would like to bring to the attention of the house include, among others, the proceedings of the house, in particular those connected with private members' bills and motions. I am not revealing any secret when I say I am not too pleased with some of the rules and regulations we have in the house governing private members' motions, bills, and requests for the production of papers. The house is not allowed to debate these matters on second reading because they are quite often ruled out of order. I think it is unfair that hon. members should be deprived of the opportunity to present their case or their grievance to the house before second reading is given. This is something that should be changed in our rules and procedures.
I should like to comment on some of my motions and bills which were introduced in

the house, particularly the bill which had to do with the building of a terminal in the town of Tisdale in the province of Saskatchewan. The intention behind the legislation that I proposed was to bring to the attention of the harbours board the need for such a terminal. I understand that the harbours board is authorized to spend this money without approval being given first by the house; they have this right by statute. What I had in mind in introducing this bill was to bring to their attention the necessity for building such a terminal. The port of Churchill on Hudson bay has a terminal with a capacity of 5 million bushels. The shipping season is very short there, only two months a year, August and September, and during the shipping season approximately 23 million bushels are exported through the port of Churchill. It has been the contention of the farmers in the west that much more grain could be shipped through this port. Some are of the opinion that as much as 40 million bushels could be shipped if we had overseas customers for such a large amount. The Hudson bay route association, and other organizations in the west, have continually asked the government to increase the terminal facilities from 5 million to 10 million bushels, but the argument against building another terminal in Churchill is that the capital expenditure of another $10 million is not justifiable or desirable because this terminal elevator would be used for only two months in the year and the present capacity of 5 million bushels is sufficient.
My argument for building another terminal in Tisdale is this. It is only about 600 miles away from Churchill, but it would be located in the centre of a farming area with an excellent wheat growing capacity and during the navigation season, namely August and September, clean grain could be shipped to Churchill, thus eliminating the loading and unloading in Churchill. In this way time would be saved. I have talked to one of the grain commissioners and he informed me that one reason not enough grain was shipped from Vancouver last year was that the grain from the prairies reached Vancouver in an unclean condition, and it takes a terrific amount of time to have this grain loaded and unloaded and cleaned. If this is the case in Vancouver, I am sure this argument could be applied in favour of the new terminal which I think should be built in Tisdale. Last year when we had this particular trouble in Vancouver, this issue was very much debated and discussed on the prairies.
As I said before, a terminal in Tisdale could provide storage facilities for 5 million bushels and it could be used 12 months in

the year, instead of having another terminal at Churchill used for only two months of the year. The argument in favour of building such a terminal is very strong. It is that if the government has to spend money on building a terminal, it might as well spend it on one that could be used 12 months in the year. The argument against building a terminal in Tisdale is that we have on the prairies three government terminals and these have never been used to full capacity. There are two terminals in Saskatchewan and one in Edmonton. The argument is that the receipt for the Saskatoon terminal for the past ten years was only an average of 2,700,000 bushels, while the capacity of the elevator is 5,500,000 bushels. The same can be said for the Edmonton elevator, as it also has only been used to half its capacity.
One reason for these elevators being used to only half their capacity over a period of ten years is that the private grain companies during the surplus years were very anxious to have their storing facilities filled to capacity, so they could collect storage charges from the government. I know from personal experience that in the northerly areas of Saskatchewan during the surplus years we were on a two bushel quota for many months -as a matter of fact, sometimes up to May- before quotas were opened, while at the same time these government terminals were standing half empty. It was a hardship to the farmers because in other areas of Saskatchewan covered by main line railway facilities they had seven and eight bushel quotas, while the people in the north were on a two bushel quota. This was of course a hardship, before we were able to bring in the consequential legislation which alleviated this situation to a certain extent, namely the interest free cash advance on farm stored grain.
My bill to build a terminal at Tisdale was ruled out of order. I wanted, first of all, to have the grain terminal built for this reason. Over the years my bill had read this way:
An act to provide for the restitution and distribution of the proceeds of grade excess and overage unlawfully confiscated and converted in 1955 and continuously thereafter under an act intituled an act to amend the Canada Grain Act to the use and purposes of the governor in council.
This meant that over the years our grain companies had always had overages which amounted to quite a large figure. I have before me statements which I should like to read into the record. In the years 1955 to 1962 overages amounted to approximately 9,975,381 bushels. Under this act these overages were supposed to belong to the governor in council. The interesting thing about the ruling which was based on the memorandum submitted by 20220-1351
The Budget-Mr. Rapp the parliamentary counsel to Mr. Speaker was that the explanatory notes were too long and that Bill No. C-245 passed on March 11, 1955 was a proper bill and that the overages shall be the property of Her Majesty. I should like to direct the attention of the house to the fact that in 1955 a similar bill was introduced and ruled out of order because the resolution preceding it had dealt with more matters than one. May I read into the record this particular quotation. Mr. Donald Fleming rose on a point of order concerning a bill No. 161 on March 5, 1957. As reported at page 1893 of Hansard the hon. member said:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. This bill, No. 161, is introduced following a resolution which was passed on February 22 and because the bill goes farther than the resolution I am taking exception to it on this point of order.
Then further on Mr. Lesage, as reported at page 1903, said that this bill was a mistake and would be withdrawn.
This, Mr. Speaker, is exactly my contention about the other bill, Bill No. 245, which was preceded by a resolution and covered more than one item, as a result of which the bill was ruled out of order. Parliamentary counsel had recommended that this bill be ruled out of order, and of course I accept the ruling. With regard to this bill introduced by Mr. Lesage which was ruled out of order, Dr. Maurice Ollivier and Mr. Batt, the assistant law clerk, gave their opinion in this way:
In our opinion, a money bill not supported by a proper resolution could be questioned in the Senate, adjudicated upon by a court of competent jurisdiction, and have moneys withheld by the proper officers under the Financial Administration Act.
The puzzling thing to me is that at the time that Dr. Ollivier ruled on this bill and Mr. Batt ruled on my bill, their opinions differed, while on a previous occasion their opinions were the same.
I am not going to argue this matter because it is now so much water under the bridge, but it is my contention that hon. members should have an opportunity to be heard when bringing these resolutions before the house so that the house knows what they are about, instead of hon. members introducing them and getting first reading, and then having them ruled out of order. I think we members of parliament are thereby deprived of an opportunity to present our case, and I urge that when the committee on procedure is convened this matter be taken up and given serious consideration. My bills were ruled out of order and they dealt with matters of great importance. At the present time western Canada is faced with a problem of great magnitude because railroads are going to

The Budget-Mr. Pearson be abandoned, some towns will almost disappear, and grain elevators will be taken away. The government should act before the farmers concerned are placed in an impossible position. It should build terminals now. We will certainly require them as our exports are increasing. These terminals should be built at once, but terminals on the west coast or at the lakehead will not serve the purpose. Inland terminals built on the prairies, however, will serve a double purpose. First of all they will give the people on the prairies an opportunity to store their grain. Second, they will give the farmers an opportunity to have their grain cleaned and shipped out and thus expedite shipment through the seaports. Although my bills have been ruled out of order I am encouraged to bring in new legislation, and I hope the government will have enough interest to pay more attention to the problems of the three western provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of participating in this budget debate as it draws to a close. I make no apology for not dealing on this occasion with the financial and economic aspects of the budget; there will be ample opportunity to do that when we discuss the budget resolutions. Perhaps I might say that I feel the budget is appropriate for the economic circumstances in which we find ourselves in Canada today-circumstances which may give us some real ground for encouragement, but which nevertheless warrant caution as we approach the future. It does not seem to me, Mr. Speaker, to be a time to bring in far reaching economic and financial changes in these circumstances, especially as we are about to receive a report from some of the most important royal commissions, in their terms of reference, which have been set up by any Canadian government for many years.
What I wish to discuss with you for a moment is a subject which has already been discussed, and rightly so, in this debate and on other occasions during this session of parliament. I refer to a problem which is very much in our minds and indeed in our hearts: the problem of Canadian unity; the problem of unity in a federation; the problem of federalism, which is basic to our growth, basic to our strength, basic to our very survival.
Politically that problem, as in every federal state, is the necessity for having a central government strong enough in jurisdiction, in resources and in resolve to discharge its responsibilities to all the people, but a central government which will not encroach on the jurisdiction of the provinces or which acts so as to prejudice their ability to do their job within their jurisdiction. The reconciliation of these two things is not easy. It

never has been, in this country or in any confederation-and I suspect it is as difficult now in Canada as it has ever been in our history.
To do its duty a central government must be strong enough to carry out the tasks imposed on it by the constitution, to provide the services for which it is responsible, especially social services, and to ensure a fair and equitable measure of comparability in respect to those services throughout the country. This country cannot survive, let alone grow, if it becomes a country of developed and underdeveloped areas-Cadillac regions and cart regions. If we allow this to happen-and I believe we will not allow it to happen-the strain on national unity, which is now great and which we all recognize, would indeed become intolerable. The federal government must also have the fiscal and financial power necessary to influence and direct national economic activities through national policies operating throughout the country in the interests of all the people. No province, no group of provinces, can do this. The federal government must be able to take new social and economic initiatives within its jurisdiction when these are necessary for the health, stability and progress of the nation as a whole. And it must be able to approach the provinces with a view to sharing with them the responsibility and the resources necessary for joint schemes of that kind.
This latter requirement brings up the whole question of shared programs about which there has been a great deal of talk, though perhaps not as much thought.
Joint federal-provincial programs, of which there are now more than 60, have been in existence in this country for many years and have proven to be a most important and useful method of bringing about balanced economic and social programs. Of course conditions are changing, not only in Canada but throughout the world and especially, perhaps, in federal states. In our own country, provinces, or some of them, are more concerned now than they used to be with the consequences of what might seem to them to be too much federal control over these programs when, as they do, they deal with matters within provincial jurisdiction. Provinces can even take this position while recognizing the value to their people of these programs. The federal government need not, of course, renew a shared program when an existing agreement comes to an end. Indeed, it can abandon, by agreement with the provinces, a shared program before an agreement is due to end under the existing arrangements.

The right of the provinces to do this, in a matter within provincial jurisdiction, we refer to as "contracting out". This is a phrase which, I confess, worries me somewhat because it gives the impression of not only contracting out of a program, but of contracting out of something which a province does not wish to see going on as an activity across Canada. Perhaps we should talk less about contracting out and more about the right of a province to take on its own responsibilities, in co-operation, if you like, with other provinces, in respect of matters which are within provincial jurisdiction. But a provincial government does have the right to opt out of programs of this kind. I believe it is proper that it should have this right, and it can do so, in our view, under certain conditions, with compensation, and convert its part of a shared program into a provincial part. For the federal government to oppose the right of a province to exercise its option of withdrawal from any joint program which covers matters under provincial jurisdiction either shared or exclusively, would not strengthen confederation; it could destroy confederation.
This does not mean, as it has been interpreted in some quarters to mean, that the federal government will encourage this course of option. But it should, I think, admit the right. Furthermore, when a province exercises its right to carry on its share of the program as a provincial program, to refuse that province financial compensation is to insist that in that province the provincial taxpayer should pay not only the full cost of the provincial program but also share the cost in the other provinces as well. Surely, no one thinks the application of this principle would strengthen confederation. When provinces, and above all the province of Quebec, question the desirability of continuing in certain joint programs they are influenced by considerations both of constitutional anxiety and by more practical matters. It is true-and so that this may be a completely non-partisan observation, let me say that the truth goes back many years-that some programs had been decided on by the federal government without adequate consultation with provincial governments. And, later, when a program begins to bear on a provincial treasury, or when provinces feel they would prefer to spend the money in question on something else, they begin to take the view-and there is ample evidence to support this-that the shared program was imposed on them rather than agreed with them. Indeed, they may also feel that the joint program has prejudiced the position of the province in question and led to the centralization of policy making and
The Budget-Mr. Pearson policy decisions in Ottawa, even in fields which are a direct responsibility of the province.
It is felt by certain provinces, and it has been felt over the years, that joint programs often do not take sufficiently into account provincial priorities. We heard a good deal about this at the most recent federal-provincial conference-that they did not take sufficiently into account provincial needs and characteristics; that there are often too many rigid federal conditions and at times irksome federal procedures.
It is certainly true, Mr. Speaker, that some joint programs have imposed increasing strains on provincial budgets and on federal budgets, but these strains have been felt most by the poorer provinces, the ones less able to bear their share of the cost. In these programs the proportion of the cost borne by a province is the same in the case of every province, unless there is a special arrangement to the contrary, and I do not know of any such arrangement.
On the other hand, it is equally true that shared cost programs, as I have already said, constitute a recognized and valuable method for making a federal system work. They have made an important contribution to the economic and social progress of our country. They have fostered national uniform standards for many important social services. For these reasons many provinces desire and advocate their continuance even though often with some changes.
Many of the disadvantages I have mentioned could be removed or reduced by the federal government working more closely with the provinces in the initiation and administration of programs. Perhaps the federal share of the cost could vary according to the fiscal capacity of the provinces participating. When a province opts out, and this is generally understood now, the conditions should not only be agreed to with that province but should not prejudice in any way the position of the provinces that remain in. With changes of this kind and the careful observance of the principles of consultation there is no reason, as I see it, why shared programs should not continue to play a useful part in our federal national development.
But I think I am safe in saying that recent experience-by "recent" I mean experience over the last year-will undoubtedly result in the federal government hesitating to embark on new shared programs without the assurance of the full and unqualified support of all the provinces. The right to opt out must be admitted, but it is much better to have a plan from which no one wants to opt out. Having said that, I do not believe that

The Budget-Mr. Pearson exercising the right of option need be disastrous or a threat to national unity. I think that is exaggerating the importance of opting out. I do admit, however, that certain disadvantages follow. When opting out takes place there always is a kind of patchwork result in the country as a whole in respect of the application of a program. This need not be disastrous but it is disadvantageous at times, and opting out does emphasize the sense of separation in our country in dealing with certain matters, especially when jurisdiction in those matters is shared. Opting out means very often that there is increased scope for federal-provincial difference over the relative advantages of staying in or opting out.
Shared programs then are one illustration, and one very much in our minds these days, of the difficulties as well as the opportunities of co-operation in the relations between the central and provincial governments in our country. These relations are in their turn a major, although not the only problem of our confederation. That problem expresses itself in political, fiscal, economic and resource development fields. It has been with us, and we should not forget this, since confederation first came into being nearly 100 years ago. Certainly in the federal government we have never in the history of our country been far away from provincial problems. These problems will remain with us as long as we are a federation, and we cannot exist as a Canadian nation except as a federation.
But while the basic problem of federalism in our country is old it has taken on new, complex and difficult forms as government at all levels has taken on more and more duties and responsibilities, especially in the field of social services. This problem has also become a part of, and indeed it is often confused with, the relations between the two foundling elements of our nation, the English speaking majority and the French speaking minority. The two problems tend to overlap and are interrelated.
The French speaking minority, as we know of course, has certain rights and privileges which are guaranteed in our constitution. It is a minority by no means confined to the province of Quebec, but that province is in a very real sense the guardian of its cultural and religious and linguistic rights. Therefore, while federal-provincial relations are an equal concern to all the provinces, and they must all be treated alike within the constitution, Quebec in a very real sense is not a province like the others. Therefore its position is bound to introduce special features into federal-provincial relationships.

For the central government to recognize the special problems arising out of the relationship with Quebec and to seek and find, whenever possible, solutions for them, without prejudicing the position of other provinces, is not capitulation or betrayal. Those who carelessly call it such are themselves, I suggest, betraying the spirit of confederation and weakening the only foundation on which confederation can stand firm and endure. A prejudiced and obstinate refusal to recognize that there are special complexities in relations with Quebec, or a failure to appreciate the special sensitiveness of that province as the guardian of the rights of a minority would soon and finally destroy confederation and make impossible the growth, in strength and unity, of a Canadian nation.
If, however, to refuse, to recognize the special position of Quebec in this way is to weaken and destroy confederation, and it could have that results, then for a province to exploit this position at the expense of Canada as a whole could have the same tragic result.
We can have no real future as a Canadian nation if we so act in our relationships provincially and federally that the result is the loosest possible kind of federation, with power and control in the hands of the provinces who would develop in their own way as best they could. I can see no salvation, I can see no survival along that course.
Of course, as we know, there are tendencies in that direction. They could destroy Canada by leading to separatism. I do not believe that these forces will prevail. We must make sure in this parliament that they do not, and in that connection the government of the day, whatever government it may be, has a very special responsibility. To this end, Mr. Speaker, this government intends to avoid either of the extreme courses I have mentioned. We propose to recognize the increasing importance of the responsibilities of the provinces in our federation, as indeed the previous government did in its financial contributions to provincial assistance.
We propose to recognize the increasing importance and responsabilities of the provinces in our federation and to help make it possible for those provinces to meet their needs by a reallocation of financial resources and a revision of our tax structure for this purpose, even if this would require a change in certain sections of our constitution, which was passed nearly 100 years ago when conditions were very different from what they are now. This is the purpose of the proposal to set up this basic tax structure committee on which I hope every province and the federal government will be represented.

In taking that attitude, surely the federal government's policy is the very oposite of centralism. We are sure, and I am sure all members of the house will share our confidence in this regard, that the provinces will use the increased authority and increased resources which they need, not to destroy but to buttress confederation. We fully appreciate, as all members of the house do, the position of the provinces. While fully appreciating that I, for one and I am sure others also, refuse to admit that the recognition of provincial rights and new provincial responsibilities requires in any way the weakening of the federal government to do its job.
This is the ultimate reconciliation we have to make in our federal system and it is one of the most difficult reconciliations that has ever been faced by any government or parliament in this country. The federal government, in these days of new responsibilities and new requirements, must also be strong in the resources it needs to deal with these increasing responsibilities, which are responsibilities of all the people of the Canadian nation from coast to coast. These facts are evident, and they must be accepted. Every province has its rights, its rights that do not change and its responsibilities that do. Every province must be in a position to exercise its rights and discharge its responsibilities, and Quebec in these matters has a special position. But equally it must be accepted and established that Canada is above all the provinces, embracing all the provinces, respecting provincial division and provincial responsibility, but that Canada, as a nation, is greater than its parts or the sum of its parts. French speaking Canada must play a proud and equal part in that nation, must feel that it belongs to Canada and that Canada from sea to sea belongs to it.
Canada is a very proud name in the world today and has been over the years. Our country need not and must not become balkanized or even, if you will pardon the expression, Aus-tro-Hungarianized. This will require understanding and, when necessary, great concessions and compromises on the part of provincial governments as well as the government in Ottawa. In other words, there must be co-operation for progress in order to avoid a conflict that would destroy us. Recent conferences with the provinces have pointed up the urgent need for such co-operation and understanding. They have also shown that without this co-operation and understanding, in the face of new pressures, tensions and problems arising out of growth and change and the quiet revolutions, the nation that our forefathers founded and built, might disintegrate and disappear. We must do
The Budget-Mr. Pearson nothing, either by provocation or by weakness or by stubborn unawareness of the basic nature of our federalism or by words or actions based on prejudice or fear, to bring about that weakening or disappearance.
We must reject the defeatism and despair which cries out that if Quebec or any other province works out an equitable arrangement by which it can take over its own share of shared programs, this means we are heading straight for separatism. This gloomy exaggeration of our difficulties may bring about the very result that those who exaggerate profess to fear. However, there can be extreme talk and extreme proposals on the other side which it would be folly and dangerous to ignore, that we can go on fragmenting ourselves, with each province ignoring the position of the other and the federal government, and the federal government ignoring the position of the provinces, and with the provinces making claims and carrying suspicions to the extreme so that they weaken the voice of Canada itself and destroy all feeling of national unity. This too, Mr. Speaker, can bring about a break-up that is not intended by those who follow such a course, except by an avowed but very small separatist minority.
Surely, it is obvious that the remedy is to avoid the paths of extremism wherever they may come from and wherever they may lead to. Mr. Mackenzie King, if I may be pardoned for quoting him, once wrote these words in a letter to a friend:
The extreme man is always more or less dangerous but nowhere more so than in politics. In a country like ours it is particularly true that the art of government is largely one of seeking to reconcile rather than to exaggerate differences.
It is the task of parliament, without regard to party; it is the challenge of statesmanship rising above faction, to find the solutions to our problems which are now more serious and more difficult than any we have faced in peacetime since 1867. We must find these solutions by agreement, not force them by compulsion. We cannot hope to find such agreement in our country if we cannot find a basis for it in our parliament.
Oh, I know, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps no one knows it much better than I, that this parliament of minorities is not an easy one for any of us, wherever we may sit. How could it be? It is idle to wrangle over blame or responsibility if parliament has, in fact, declined in repute over the last ten years and particularly, if you like, over the last two.
I am quite willing to accept, for my party and for myself, our share of any blame and responsibility; to acknowledge both political the parliamentary sins of commission and

The Budget-Mr. Pearson omission, in opposition and in government. Every party, every leader and every parliament in our history has had much to its or his credit, and things also to its or his discredit. But it is well to keep a sense of perspective when we try to analyse our own faults and achievements. It is well also, for those of us who analyse them, to keep a sense of perspective, and a knowledge of history, which I should not talk about, helps to maintain a sense of perspective.
For one thing, we should realize that circumstances and conditions governing the functioning of parliament today, especially in the realm of communication, have changed radically in the last 30, 40 and 50 years. The media of communication and commentary can now bring our weaknesses and misdeeds, and occasionally even our achievements, into every home, immediately and with a dramatic effect not possible many years ago.
But while perspective can give us some comfort because it helps us to emphasize and maintain a sense of proportion, perspective can be damaging and, indeed, can be dangerous if it is allowed to obscure the fact that, while we may not be any worse, or even as bad as our forefathers in politics and in parliament, today we must be better because the problems we now face are far greater in degree and in complexity than theirs, and the penalty for failure to deal with them is correspondingly greater.
That is why we are all anxious, in all parties in the house, to take steps-and I hope we can agree on them-whereby parliament can operate more effectively in the interests, not of parliamentarians but of the people of the country, and that is why all of us attach very great importance to the committee on procedure which we have set up, and which I venture to hope will be submitting to us, before many days, an interim report which, if it can be agreed upon by all of us-and I hope it can-would do something to improve our procedure and make it more effective, pending the final report of that committee.
We must then, Mr. Speaker, do everything we can by our conduct in parliament to justify parliament as an institution and to bring it into better repute than it seems to have attained recently.
Our major problem today, and these are my closing words, Mr. Speaker, is not one of nation building. Although we still have that, and although Canadians have achieved great success in the field of nation building ever since 1867 right down to 1964, our problem today is not one of nation building; it is a problem of nation saving. It is not less


than that-saving this nation from forces that weaken and could ultimately destroy it, forces all the more dangerous because they are used often by those who do not desire that result.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this parliament can strengthen Canada and, by strengthening it, we can certainly save it. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is above all partisan, selfish, regional and provincial considerations.

PROVISION TO ENABLE CIVIL SERVANTS TO ENGAGE IN POLITICAL ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-10, to enable civil servants to engage in political activity.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my purpose in introducing this bill this afternoon is that by so doing I hope we can initiate a discussion in the house about a very grave and serious problem. By that, I am referring to the political and civic rights of the civil servants of Canada.
There are approximately 200,000 people in this category, and at the present time they are in a state of virtual suspended animation with regard to political activity. This situation arises as a result of the Civil Service Act which was passed in 1960-61, and more particularly as a result of section 61 of the act, which provides as follows:
(1) No deputy head or employee shall
(a)	engage in partisan work in connection with any election for the election of a member of the House of Commons, a member of the legislature of a province or a member of the council of the Yukon Territory or the Northwest Territories; or
(b)	contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for the funds of any political party.

Subsection 2 of this section provides that anyone who violates this is liable to be dismissed, and the act properly goes on to provide that persons so charged cannot be dismissed unless they have an opportunity to be heard, themselves, and through representatives.
The net effect of this provision is to deprive our civil servants in toto of the right to engage in any form of political activity. The section of course is somewhat vague. It would appear that a civil servant could engage in political activity so long as it was not at election time, and provided he did not contribute any money to a political party. It would also appear that a civil servant could engage in partisan work for any sort of party he wished, no matter how extreme its views, provided it did not run candidates. However, as I have said, the net effect is to place a blanket denial on the rights of our civil servants to engage in political activity. The section does not define "partisan work" very clearly, but I feel from reviewing the events that over the years a very narrow definition has grown up as to what constitutes partisan work. Many civil servants are very doubtful if they even have the right to be seen at a political meeting. Readings of Hansard indicate that even a civil servant having his picture taken might constitute grounds for dismissal. It is interesting to note that as late as 1957 civil servants could be dismissed on the charge by a member of parliament that they had engaged in partisan activity, and indeed this could be done without any investigation at all.
I am merely saying that by our legislative act we have to all intents and purposes isolated the civil servant from political activity. This is to me a very serious limitation that we have placed upon their rights as citizens in a democracy, and it can only be justified if some more overriding reasons can be advanced. I would like to see us discuss whether these overriding reasons still exist, because certainly this is not the kind of restriction which any of us would tolerate were it imposed by private industry, trade unions or farm organizations which employ people. It is my contention that the time has come for the relaxation of this very rigid rule even though there are still some areas where it may have to be applied. Thus clause 2 of the bill provides:
Notwithstanding anything contained in any other act of parliament, every employee of Her Majesty in right of Canada, shall have the right to engage in any form of political activity-
Then I have set out some of the categories:
(a)	the right freely to associate with others in political parties and organizations;
(b)	the right to speak, to write, and to publish on behalf of candidates for public office;
Civil Servants in Politics
(c)	the right to be a candidate for public office; and
(d)	the right to make contributions to and expenditures on behalf of political parties and candidates for public office-
It is also provided in the bill that of course no such employee shall use his hours of employment or any of the tools of his office for these purposes, and clause 4 provides:
The provisions of this act shall not apply to:
(a)	a deputy head as defined in paragraph (h) of subsection 1 of section 2 of the Civil Service Act, or an employee of equivalent rank; or
(b)	an employee employed in a confidential capacity.
It seems to me this is the only limitation which we can now justify with respect to political activity by civil servants. The policy of political neutrality has had a long tradition not only in our parliament here in Canada but of course in the United Kingdom as well. But in the United Kingdom they have questioned the advisability of perpetuating the blanket nature of the prohibition. The matter was discussed in a very interesting book by the late Harold J. Laski called "Reflections on the constitution". In that book Mr. Laski re-examines the political and civil rights of civil servants and makes some conclusions. He says:
I think It is absurd to insist that, once a civil servant, not in the industrial grades, becomes a candidate for parliament he shall resign his post. I think it is even more absurd to lay it down that civil servants shall not play a part, in their leisure time, in the political organization in which they believe.
He deals with the French system where a great many civil servants have played an important part in the politics of their nation. He mentions in particular Mr. Leon Blum. These civil servants have played their part in the politics of their nation and it has not interfered with their impartiality nor with their ability to discharge their role as civil servants. He felt that below the capacities that I have mentioned it is enough if an official of the particular class gives an undertaking, whether he becomes a parliamentary candidate or takes an active interest in his party, not to discuss in public the affairs of the department to which he belongs, nor to reveal information which he obtains by virtue of his position in the service. He felt it would be sufficient to give this undertaking, and any violation of it might constitute grounds for dismissal.
Indeed, the British have progressed ever further in this field. The Whitley council examined this whole problem of the political rights of civil servants and they advised a horizontal division where some are completely free to engage in political activity, some are more restricted and some are barred. I disagree thoroughly with that contention. The wording of section 61,

I am certainly sure that no hon. member would discourage an association from trying to express its opinion on the principle whether or not the legislation as presently constituted is adequate to protect the rights of civil servants.
This question may be looked at from several different points of view. The hon. member who has spoken referred to the point of view of an individual civil servant and a citizen in the community. That is of course a valid point of view, but we must also look at the point of view and rights of a government. We must look too at the point of view of political parties and at the needs and rights of political parties. And not the least, I think we must look at the public interest which dictated this particular section in the first instance.
If the hon. member was calling attention to a matter which had not been reviewed by this house during a period of time within the living memory of members of this house and had been long standing on the statute books, I think there would be even more justification for raising the subject. But as recently as 1960, when a comprehensive review of the Civil Service Act was enacted by this house, the clause to which the hon. member referred was reviewed and modified, as he acknowledged, to give a much greater degree of democratic control. For example, a man or woman may not be dismissed except after formal inquiry. No longer do the rather discriminatory provisions concerning complaints by members of parliament apply. If he had cited any injustices under the application of the rule I would have been more moved by his arguments.
As the situation stands today there is no question that the government faces something of a dilemma. Political activity in our society relies on the spontaneous and voluntary action of citizens who put themselves in the position of assuming a greater degree of responsibility for the kind of government and society in which they live. That is basic to any democratic society. We must have a maximum voluntary involvement of citizens in those activities. We want to encourage the government. At the same time the government as an employer must set the example of a good employer. As the hon. member pointed out, we want employers to encourage their employees to take part in politics. Politics in a democratic society would be meaningless without this participation.
That is one side of the question. The other side concerns the history of activity which

Civil Servants in Politics brought such a regulation on to the books in the first instance. The Canadian civil service has since 1920 built a reputation which is second to that of no other country in the world in terms of competence, respect for the merit principle, in terms of the encouragement of men and women of profound ability to seek a career in the public service of Canada and to develop a career in a way which makes us as Canadians proud of their talents. If this rule had had the effect of substantially discouraging numbers of men and women of prominence from seeking a public career because they would feel they were in a sense second class citizens and would forfeit their full rights, then I think the hon. member would have made something of a case. But the opposite is the fact. The profound respect for the merit principle and the degree to which it was applied and respected, in Canada even more so than in many contemporary democracies in the western world, has had the effect of encouraging large numbers of competent people to seek a career in the public service.
There are, of course, evils when political activity takes place within the public service. History prior to 1920 discloses examples. Evils manifest themselves as abuses of individuals by unscrupulous members of political parties, and there are persons who participate in public life who are not of the sort of standing which we should like to see. There is the opportunity for a more or less compulsory political contribution; there is the opportunity of calling for a return for services rendered. This is the situation when men and women, who show up at election time and make their careers in the public service, then go to their members of parliament and say: I worked for you; now you work for me. If anyone wants to read the reports which formed part of the background of the first civil service act in 1920 and the disrepute into which it brought the civil service as it existed prior to that date, he will find ample confirmation of these points.
The other side of the coin is the abuse of civil servants in circumstances in which financial contributions could or might be invited. I note that the hon. member has not spoken of the role of the civil servants staff associations, where they are free to take an active part on behalf of, or against, any particular political party. It seems to me this whole field would bear careful examination.
We must bear in mind the tradition of neutrality which exists in the civil service- the tradition of loyalty to the government of the day whatever its political complexion; the tradition of the protection of the rights of

individual civil servants against unscrupulous holders of public office. These are the reasons for the rule. These are the reasons why parliament in the sixties did review sections of the act and introduced some changes, though not the changes suggested by the hon. member.
A great deal more could be said about political activity which is not of a political partisan nature. I refer to political activity among civil servants, especially at municipal level. I think the tradition of non-participation in the Canadian civil service is so strong that it leads to inhibition in areas where there is no need for it. This is not a matter of law. I think it is a matter of the development of practice and, in particular, of administrative practice. In a city such as the national capital, where a municipal form of government is maintained, this practice has had the effect of discouraging men and women, among them some of the most vigorous and most able people in Canada, from offering themselves for office. It is not the law that is responsible for this. It is a tradition which has grown up within a general interpretation of the law. During the 1962 federal election, in the course of the campaign, a member of the civil service commission made a public statement to the effect that wives of civil servants should have nothing to do with politics. And the inference was left that close relatives of civil servants should also think twice about doing so. There is nothing in the law or in the regulations that says this. But this type of administrative interpretation by a responsible head of the public service, in this case a member of the civil service commission, is to be roundly condemned as leading to a situation which is creating an evil. The law which is presently on the books has not, in my experience, been the object of a great deal of criticism. I am not aware that any gross inequities have arisen. There is an excessive timidity about offering oneself as a candidate, for example, for the office of alderman on a local council, or for office as reeve or urban councillor in smaller municipalities.
Here the important question is a question of possible conflict of duties and, in addition, the level of responsibility that is assumed. It is reasonable to expect that when a man or woman is hired by the public service for full time work his employer has a right to full time service. Frequently, service on a council creates obligations in terms of conflicts of time, or even conflicts of energy. This imposes a problem, and administrative discretion has to be exercised. It is perfectly lawful and, I believe, it is to be encouraged that civil servants who do not experience

a conflict with their jobs should offer themselves for municipal office on a non-partisan basis. If they like that kind of life they can quit their jobs and take up politics as a full time occupation. Later, if they find they do not like it as well as they had imagined they would, they can go back, qualify themselves by passing open competitions and re-enter the public service, if that is what they wish to do. There is nothing wrong in that, nor should it be discouraged.
As a matter of administrative practice, treasury board has set a limit of earnings above which it has not been the practice to grant leave of absence so that a man or woman might offer himself as a candidate. That level is revised from time to time. It currently reflects the average earnings of an alderman in one of the larger cities of Ontario or Quebec. The level is drawn so as to discourage those who might wish to serve on the board of control in, for example, Toronto, Ottawa, Sudbury or Hamilton, because the board of control, as the cabinet of the city, is very much a full-time responsibility though its members are seldom paid on a full-time basis. It is therefore necessary for men and women wishing to carry out duties at this level to avail themselves of leave of absence. I think it should be the policy of the government to grant such leave of absence in the overwhelming majority of the cases in which application is made.
What is wrong with these rules? I know that the government, as an employer, in terms of being a custodian of the civil rights of its employees, seeks to give the maximum encouragement to those wishing to take part in political activities. But the public has a right, too. The public has a right to expect that its employees will show equal loyalty to whatever government is in power. The Civil Service Act permits civil servants to contest elected offices at the municipal level. Indeed, it encourages them to do so. This type of activity provides a way by which participants can be initiated, if they seek this kind of life. As for the stage at which a man or woman takes on a political label and offers himself or herself as a candidate for a particular political party, I think that is the stage at which our legislation draws the line. I do not see anything terribly wrong with this. It is perfectly all right for a man who wants to run in the name of a party to quit his job-after all, he is a free agent-and then, if he decides he does not like political life, he can enter another competition held on the merit principle, and rest assured that he will not be the object of discrimination because of the fact that he participated in political activity.
