Mr. Speaker, I regret that I did not know earlier that this bill would be coming up today because I should have liked to examine more closely the problems it would create. However, from what he has said, it would seem that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) wishes to give greater importance to members of parliament than to civil servants.
Now, it is well known that at the federal level, civil servants play an exceedingly important role as compared with members of parliament. In fact, they have a role to play and they can remove themselves from the influence not of politics, I would say, but of parliament itself. Thus, very often when we ask for the reasons behind a certain decision, we are told that the letter was based on confidential documents containing information which cannot be revealed to private members of parliament. However, civil servants for their part may not only have information but may also create situations about which we should require explanations.
As far as the civil service is concerned, I believe its powers are exceedingly important and something might indeed be done about it. I make this statement, knowing quite well it is not very wise, politically speaking, but I wonder whether an inquiry into the administration of the civil service would not be justified to find out whether

Civil Servants in Politics there are not some nooks and corners where some dust may have collected and where a little dusting would be useful.
The civil service is protected by the civil service commission, on which no political pressure is being exerted. This, I admit. However, the complaints received from civil servants holding subordinate positions are so frequent-I would even say they are almost incessant

that, in my opinion, it would be wise to study the suggestion I made a moment ago, that is to conduct an inquiry into the administration of the civil service.
The hon. member stated a few moments ago that if civil servants were not allowed to enter politics, they would be deprived of their rights. I do not know any civil servant who was ever compelled to enter the civil service. When entering the civil service, he knew what to expect. He knew he was to work for his country or his province, as the case may be. He knew also that his position involved some duties which were constantly to be respected and that some rights which he considered legitimate were to be denied him, in many circumstances, and this, for reasons of security or confidentiality. This means the applicant for a civil service job knew what to expect.
On the other hand, if he wanted to engage in political activities, if he wished to express his views to the people as a whole, all he had to do was to go into politics and run as a member of such and such a party. If he had no desire to belong to any party, he could have run as an independent.
I do not feel those are sufficient reasons to require that an act of parliament allow public servants to engage in political activity. But, as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) said a while ago, I think there is a distinction to be made between municipal politics, school politics and even, in some respects, provincial politics, because the ties between federal and provincial parties are so close that I would be afraid to allow a public servant to engage in political activity in one of those two fields.
As far as municipal and school board politics are concerned, I do not feel we can prevent a civil servant who undoubtedly has the necessary qualifications from taking an active part in such activities. In fact, if a civil servant wishes to hold public office, I do not see why we should refuse him permission to do so.
However, when it is said that civil servants are deprived of any chance to be helpful to the government and parliament, I feel, as I said a moment ago, that that is granting little importance to members of parliament, considering especially the fact that those people can be of use to the government.


In fact, if a committee of the house needs information, it is easy to call in competent officials and ask them to explain matters for the benefit of the members of the committee who will later on make recommendations to parliament and to the government.
The government and parliament can make full use of those people if they have qualifications. I fail to see why they would be better qualified simply because they would work actively for a political party. For a long time, when law clerks or certain judges were to be appointed, for instance, they were required to belong to a political party and, very often, it was the only qualification required. This gave rise to more and more complaints. Yet, some people would like to require from civil servants, on top of necessary qualifications, membership in a political party.
Mr. Speaker, I think that such an argument is illogical and it should at least be criticized before it is accepted.
It must also be recognized that in spite of the sacrosanct independence of the civil service commission, as I was saying, there is surely some way for politics to intervene, because too many civil servants come to see their members to ask them to bring some pressure to bear so that they may be appointed to such and such a position. That means that to get into the civil service, political influence is often used, but once the candidate gets in, if he wants to remain there, he must get completely out of politics.
If he wants to go into active politics, the only way would be to quit the civil service and take a chance, as everybody else does, by running at a general election.
As far as I am concerned, I could not serve two masters.
When I chose to devote myself to politics, I forced myself to give up the practice of medicine, not because I was no longer capable of practising, but because I felt my first duty was to my country and my constituents. That means that the right I actually have to practise medicine is restricted and also minimized by my new duties as a member of this house.
I feel that should apply also to a civil servant who would be allowed to engage in political activity.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to labour the point, for I know other members would like to speak on this matter and, especially, that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) would like to obtain the consent of the house to refer his bill to a special committee.
Still, I should like to say that if, under a socialist or ultra-socialist regime, it is quite normal for civil servants to engage in politics since the latter then become a direct function

of the government, the intrusion of politics in the public service is absolutely unthinkable in a democracy like ours where the individual still has, in his riding or at the polling booth the apparent right to choose the men who will form the government.
Obviously, a civil servant's political affiliations may play against him if he has been or still is engaged in politics. If there is a change of government, he will be the first to suffer.
This new measure might keep the government and the whole parliament from using the services of a very qualified man.
Mr. Speaker, I do not say that I am totally opposed to the fact that civil servants might engage in political activities-as I said earlier, at some levels, it is quite possible-but I object to the general principle and I should like very much to have the opportunity of discussing the matter in committee, if ever this bill should go before one.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENABLE CIVIL SERVANTS TO ENGAGE IN POLITICAL ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out as definitely as I can that we, sitting on this side of the house, take the introduction of this bill by a member of the New Democratic party as a compliment to our cabinet and to the Liberal government which the country is enjoying today. It would appear that with a Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who came directly from the civil service into the arena of federal politics, and a Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who came directly into politics from the civil service, the mover of the bill appreciates the abilities and qualities of such leadership and is endeavouring to increase the number of civil servants who might engage in federal politics for the good of the country.
This principle has been demonstrated by the activities of such former civil servants as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), who is measuring up to the peerless stature of the late C. D. Howe. We have, as Minister of Industry and Defence Production (Mr. Drury), a former civil servant, who is establishing new records in that division. We have a Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) straight out of the civil service, and I understand he has had 14 years of continuous service in either provincial or federal civil service positions. He is a man of experience and ability. It is a very nice tribute to our cabinet and to the Liberal government of the day to have the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) introduce a bill which he hopes will enlarge the number of civil servants coming into the area of federal politics.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENABLE CIVIL SERVANTS TO ENGAGE IN POLITICAL ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
But not from the Liberal party.
Civil Servants in Politics

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENABLE CIVIL SERVANTS TO ENGAGE IN POLITICAL ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
However, I cannot say that all ventures of this nature have been for the good of the country. There are occasions on record-I do not wish to be too specific- where civil servants, as a result of the nature of their occupation as relief administrators or as inspectors for this and that, travelling around at government expense and making contact with thousands of voters, have established in that manner a popularity which has enabled them to run for office. This has been done by passing out government money in one way or another. One might almost say the government has subsidized their campaign throughout the years they were engaged as civil servants.
I do not believe that federal civil servants should be eligible to participate in federal politics. I do believe that a dominion government employee should take part in provincial politics and municipal politics. I do believe that a provincial civil servant should take part in municipal politics and federal politics. I do not believe a civil servant should engage in politics at the level at which the parliament or legislature of which he would be a member would be his employer. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) has pointed out that he believes there are many people who are afraid to engage in political action because they know they are forbidden to take part in some fields of endeavour, and therefore they refuse to take part in the much wider field.
It strikes me that there must be a tremendous number of people in this country who are quite willing to become civil servants. As the last speaker pointed out, despite the restrictions on political activities, people are willing to become civil servants. It is interesting to bear in mind at this time the remarks made by the Minister of Industry only last week when he pointed out that there were 6,500 applications received by the civil service commission for the 87 positions advertised in the Department of Industry. If 6,500 Canadian people are willing to apply for 87 positions that are open, despite the restrictions that now exist on political activities, this would indicate to me, if not to other members of the house, that these people are willing to accept these restrictions which have been imposed for some years. The onus cannot be very serious or we would not have had that number of applications for these few positions.
Indeed, many men and women have not been deprived of taking part in election campaigns because they were civil servants. The late Mr. Raymond, who was Liberal member for the city of Brantford for many years, was the former postmaster of the city of Brantford. Some of you may recall this

Civil Servants in Politics gentleman as the blind member of parliament who, for a number of years, would stand in this house and correct any misquotation by calling the speaker's attention to the fact that the next paragraph read as follows. His memory was phenomenal and his literary knowledge was vast. He was a former civil servant who made his mark in the federal field. It is true he gave up his position to run, but this did not restrict him in running for parliament.
We have in this house many former government employees. I do not like to limit the words "civil servant" to the federal civil servants. We have provincial civil servants; we have municipal civil servants; we have federal civil servants. Now that we have the United Nations, we will be getting international civil servants. Men and women can take part in various levels of political activity. In my own riding of York-Humber I have about one eighth of the area of the township of Etobicoke, which has a population of 173,000 souls. I am sure it will interest members of parliament to know that one local-I will not say problem, I will say question-concerns the fact that the board of education in that township is pretty well dominated by teachers. These teachers are not in the employ of the board of education of Etobicoke. They are men and women, university professors, who are employees of other boards of education or universities elsewhere in metropolitan Toronto. However, since they live in Etobicoke, they are qualified to run for office there.
We have this little question as to whether or not teachers should be allowed to run for boards of education in municipalities where they are not teaching, which pinpoints the problem that is brought to the fore by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) in introducing this bill. The reeve of Scarborough, in metropolitan Toronto, is one of the ablest reeves Scarborough has ever seen or will see, and he is a former high school teacher, Mr. Albert Campbell. He is a credit to the community and is building up Scarborough's reputation as reeve.
The Prime Minister of this country and myself were boys together in the city of Peterborough, and when we were children one of the finest mayors there, and prior to that an alderman, was Mayor Buller, who was collector of customs in Peterborough customs house for many, many years. He was a civil servant but he contributed much to the growth of Peterborough and the country by engaging in political activity.
When I was a child, visiting my grandparents here in Ottawa, I heard great praise heaped on a school teacher in Kent school, who for years was a very useful member


of the city council of Ottawa and, if I am not mistaken, rose to be controller. He was an employee of the public school board who was taking a very active part in municipal politics on the council level.
In our Liberal party on this side of the house I am pleased that we have such members as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty), the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter), all former school teachers, or school principals, or school inspectors. They have not been held back in the field of federal politics because they were former school teachers.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) also was a former school teacher. I call him a former civil servant. Many people state that an employee of a board of education is not a civil servant, but I point out that he is in receipt of tax moneys. At one time the former hon. member for the city of Peterborough, Mr. Pitman, was a high school teacher and is a high school teacher again. These men had much to contribute to the communities in which they were teaching and they took part in federal politics with credit to themselves.
The former prime minister of this country appointed a C.N.R. employee to the Senate. That is a crown corporation and you can call him a civil servant; but he made his mark. He contributed much to the province of Ontario, to the Dominion of Canada, and now has a seat in the other place. I would remind you of the present minister of education in the province of Ontario, a former crown attorney in the county of Peel. He gave up his position as crown attorney and sought elective public office in the provincial field. He became a member of the legislature and a member of the cabinet, and today is a good servant of the public in the form of minister of education, despite the fact that some years ago he was a civil servant as crown attorney for Peel.
I cannot see that the civil service employees of this country, whether on the municipal, provincial or federal level, are suffering under the laws that now exist. The town of Weston is one of the five communities making up the riding of York-Humber. An alderman there for some time and a reeve for many years was a pilot on T.C.A. It is a crown corporation, but no one held it against that gentleman that he was an employee of a crown corporation. He was elected to public office year after year in Weston, and served with great distinction to the town of Weston and to metropolitan Toronto, of which Weston is a part.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Can-telon) is a former school teacher who is a

credit to Kindersley and is of value to this house. The hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Weichel) is a former federal civil servant. He has been elected more than once from his riding, which shows the regard in which he is held. It is not any terrible onus that is placed on these civil servants that there are some restrictions on their political activities in the laws of the land. They can engage in political activities with credit to themselves, and if they wish to run for public office I do believe they are willing to offer themselves and suffer the consequences if they are defeated.
It is difficult at this time to recall the names of many defeated candidates for public office, but we know the civil servants who have been elected to this house, because there are only 265 to consider when discussing a bill of this nature. I am certain, however, that there were many former civil servants who offered their services and, because they were not successful at the polls, were able to return to their former positions or to some other positions they had secured.
With regard to civil servants, I have been thinking of what the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Francis) drew to our attention, that people supported him and, after his election, came around and pointed out they worked for him and wanted his help to get them a position in the civil service.
Talking about restrictions on government jobs, how would we like to have men coming off the bench of the Supreme Court of Canada, or the Ontario supreme court bench, and offering themselves for public office? We hold all members of the bench up to praise and we point out how fair they are and how impartial they are in all their actions and decisions. I do not think for one moment it would be proper for us to give the right to men to come off the bench and run for public office, men whose reputation the country as a whole builds up since we must hold our judges and justices in the highest respect. It would not be right for such judges and justices whose reputations have been built up for them by the taxpayers, who in their exalted positions have travelled around as trial judges, and in doing so have met thousands of people, to engage in federal or provincial politics, after spending those years of activity on the bench.
I cannot see any reason for making any alterations at this time in the laws as they now exist. With 6,500 applications for 87 positions, and every one of the 6,500 knowing these restrictions exist at the present time, we have our answer definitely there.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted the other day where a British historian had written that British general elections were locks on the canal of British progress. I was going to start tonight by suggesting that our elections were locks, period, and by scorching the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and to a lesser extent the Leader of the Opposition on the basis that while the one dallied and the other raised Cain, and both gave us fine words, on our major problem, which is national survival, the situation seemed to be worsening. But the Prime Minister's speech this afternoon, which was quite candid, certainly constructive and somewhat conciliatory to some of us who were critical of him in this field, has made me certain that he does know the dangers and does feel they are matters which time and negotiation will solve, and that he and all of us have a concept of Canadianism which enables us to join with him in fighting for it.
I was moved to consider being sharp not least by an article sent to me from Paris- I got it today-which appeared in Le Monde last Sunday, April 12, headed "Les relations entre Quebec et Ottawa ont atteint un inquie-tant degre de tension" and written by the Le Monde correspondent in Quebec, Jean Tainturier. It is a very long article analysing what he calls the disquieting degree of tension between Quebec and Ottawa, and it seemed to me that the last paragraph was the kind of call to arms to which I think the Prime Minister will listen. I hope my fellow members will forgive my pronunciation:

The unrest concerning the constitution which has developed during the last few years has thereby reached a dangerous phase from which the breaking up process of the Canadian confederation could spring unless bold measures are quickly taken by Ottawa.
2156	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fisher

In other words, this gentleman recommends an audacious or bold and rapid seizing of initiative by Ottawa, and I am in hopes that the Prime Minister's remarks this afternoon are an indicator of this. I also endorse the remarks made by my hon. friend for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron), who made the point as one of the generation which bled so much in the first war that he and his colleagues of that generation had a bill to present to this country in terms of asking us, those of us who came afterwards, not to deal with this matter in terms of insult.
I was somewhat shocked to discover a few weeks ago when I read an article about myself in a magazine by the name of "Actu-alite", written by Jean Marc Poliquin, that he used the adjective "brutal" a number of times to describe my attitude in so far as French Canada is concerned. I have always tried in this particular matter, as an individual and a party spokesman, to be frank. I certainly hope that tonight and at any other time in the future I will take heed of the words of my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and will not do anything to exacerbate the difficulties or trade in insults.
The Prime Minister's speech today gave us a bit of a framework and an undertaking, but I think he would be the first to concede that he did not do much more than that. He left us with some questions which will puzzle us until he and his colleagues give us more reasons. He gave us a good outline of the difficulties of joint programming. He suggested that "opting out" was a better phrase than "contracting out" of joint programs between the federal government and the government of a province. Then toward the end of his speech he mentioned that what the two governments consider to be the French and English factor in Canada in language terms really was something different that could not be matched up with the joint programs or anything like this. He indicated, just as we believe and it is in our program, that there should be a special status for Quebec because of its language and culture responsibility. But some of the questions that are left unanswered, for example, are: Where does the federal member from Quebec stand? As far as that is concerned, where does the federal member from Ontario stand on something like the pension plan when, without anything we can do or say about it, the initiative in this specific case has been seized by a provincial premier?
I am not going to raise the question; I just want to circle around the fact of where


do we vote if we are going to be representing people who in effect have a premier who leads them in other matters and says that the federal government shall not enter, or may not enter here and become involved in this particular problem. It seems to me that a member from Ontario faces something that is quite difficult with regard to the pension plan. For the French Canadian member from Quebec who represents his people here and who sees the provincial premier claiming that the primary, or the basic, or the fundamental responsibility for speaking for French Canada does not enter into this chamber at Ottawa but rests with the legislative assembly at Quebec, I know there are a great many problems and difficulties.
It seems to me that in working out this special status for Quebec the Prime Minister has to determine who has the delegation of authority both from us and from the other provincial governments to deal with Quebec. If Quebec is given a special status, what devolves upon us-that is, upon the federal parliament and authority-regarding two matters; for example, the minorities in Quebec and the minorities of French Canadians in the rest of the country? I want, and my party wants, to respect the rights of the French under the constitution in the rest of the country, but if they are to receive more privileges than they have now-that is, the French outside of Quebec-for example in the fields of language rights, education or provincial politics, it becomes again a matter for the provinces rather than the federal government. After all, the Prime Minister is not in a position to undertake what may be given in Ontario with regard to educational or language rights for French Canadians. If Quebec's special status is recognized, what do we do to keep Quebec representation in this house with some kind of prestige and authority? Members may not believe it, but I actually feel, not anything so high handed or high headed as pity or something like that, but I do feel grieved and sorry for my colleagues from Quebec when I realize that they are under pressure and, in a way, under attack and I would suggest that they are less representative of their people than are other representatives gathered in this place.
The Prime Minister's approach as he outlined it today was a pragmatic and empirical one with the idea that we negotiate around a table and bargain step by step; that we have to go slowly and there needs to be a great many compromises. This is all very well, and it is certainly in the Canadian tradition. But emotionally it seems to me that our Quebec friends may be too impatient for this. English speaking Canada at the present time, as I tend to feel it, is also working up something

that is emotional and imaginative with regard to this whole matter. One wonders what happens if things do boil more toward fever heat. What more immediate steps can be taken than those the Prime Minister outlined, which really depend upon a long, slow series of negotiations and deals and compromises. It seems to me that we need to be prepared for this. I sometimes get the feeling-I do not know whether other people in the house join me in this-that the politicians in the province of Quebec may be riding a juggernaut for which they had not any reins. I do not say this in order to irritate, but I just raise this as a question that may put more urgency into this whole matter than the approach that was given today by the Prime Minister.
There is one other point that needs to be made in regard to this question. I wish my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) were here because it is the one thing that is always more before him than anything else. The Liberal party has always claimed some kind of prior magic or mesmerism in regard to handling the French Canadian representation. I think there are claims being made at the present time, and if some of us laugh it is rather hollow laughter in view of the fact that the Liberal party is having the same difficulties that other parties are having.
I suggest that at this time when emotions and feelings of nationalism are not confined to Quebec it would be well for the Liberal party, as the federal Liberal administration, no matter what happens in its detachment from the Quebec Liberal party, to take the attitude that it did not have all the answers unto itself in this matter. Otherwise it seems to me that it is fruitless for the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to come to the house and appeal for our help and support, if at the same time his hustings speakers are going round and saying things such as that said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) a few weeks ago, that the Liberal party is the only hope to save confederation. I make this point in some earnestness, Mr. Speaker, because one of the most difficult problems ahead with regard to solving the confederation difficulty is this whole question of partisan claims.
One of the last points I wish to make in relation to this matter has come to me in my reading from a book called "Beyond the ruling class" by Suzanne Keller, and it seems to me that this is one point which we should bring to the minds of the provincialists and the premiers of the provinces at this time. This writer makes the point of the experience of Greece in the fifth century B.C. and that of Rome in the fifth century A.D. She says:
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
In each case the failure to control and curb the desires for local autonomy accelerated the decline of these civilizations. The inability to transcend sectional interests has plagued primitive societies as well, many of whom must manage to solve these problems without benefit of inclusive political organization. Various alternative measures-strict village exogamy, or membership in age-sets that override local village loyalties on specific occasions, or membership in far-flung trading associations-might be considered functional equivalents of political organizations such as the state.
Advanced industrial societies, it appears, are currently on the way toward ever larger, functional divisions. This trend was anticipated by Saint-Simon, among others, who envisaged an international order based not on national but occupational co-ordination. Durkheim continued this line of thought. He favoured the displacement of segmental, territorial solidarity by a comprehensive, functional solidarity based on occupational interdependence, residence becoming less and occupation more important. "A day will come," he prophesied, "when our social and political organization will have a base exclusively, or almost exclusively, occupational". Increasingly it does appear as if local trading, academic, artistic, financial, and fashion centres are yielding ground, and territorial solidarities are making way for other kinds.
This is so obvious in North America that it hardly needs telling, and yet at this time we are making what in essence are demands across the board because of our fragmented political society. We are giving rise to a parochial autonomy.
I now want to refer briefly to Ontario's attitude toward the pension plan. I read recently an article by Bruce MacDonald in the Globe and Mail entitled "Robart's pension reversal", and it made me feel that I was completely wrong about Premier Robarts. I had a suspicion that he was interested in taking a stand which would be in line with the private insurance companies of Canada. He was against larger contributions. I thought he wanted smaller benefits. Now it seems he wants larger contributions and greater benefits and more investment moneys. This is an indication that Premier Robarts may be almost a blooming socialist. It almost indicates that he has been under the influence of the Swedes. Because if you stop and figure the line that Mr. Robarts is now taking-and Mr. MacDonald has outlined it very well-almost everything which Mr. Robarts now seems to be saying, although it does not square very well with what he said before, is an indicator that he is taking the long term attitude of the social democrats in Europe whereby investment from pension funds is one of the great big things you go for.
The other surprising thing to me, and very pleasing of course, is that he seems to want greater benefits, earlier benefits, more survivors' benefits, and of course this fits in with larger contributions. This remarkable about-face by Premier Robarts is something that we
2158	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fisher need to know a great deal more about. But at the present time, from looking at what he seems to be intending, we almost have an indicator that all the long propaganda efforts of Donald MacDonald and his fellows in the provincial legislature are bearing fruit and that we now have a conservative who is recognizing the merits of social democratic pension attitudes.
One further point in connection with the pension plan is the attitude of the teachers federation. I think this is a glorious demonstration of inconsistency. In effect I have been a member of the teachers federation. They are a closed shop. You have to belong to them and pay a fee, and they have had a nice arrangement with the provincial government that whenever the school trustees in Ontario wanted provincial-wide bargaining in terms of salaries the great cry has gone up by the school teachers: "Oh no, we must keep it within the municipal boundaries. This is the authority by which education has been set in this province, and therefore we should and must keep it that way".
This is very good, Mr. Speaker, from what you might call the trade union point of view. You keep the bargaining unit small. You have a closed shop and you have the benefit of the whole federation across the provinces behind you. You separate the boards one by one and gradually work up over the years to a better salary standard. The Ontario teachers federation has done a magnificent job in this regard, and as one of the former members I was complementary to them when I belonged and I am complementary to them now.
Now they come out against the Canada pension plan and their argument is that it must be set within the provincial framework. They are provincialists where the pension plan is concerned. They are such provincialists that they go out of their way, on a matter in which they have no confidence and I would think a great deal of ignorance, to slur and slight our unemployment insurance plan in an effort somehow to indicate that the unemployment insurance plan is not working and is a failure. I just wanted to put that inconsistency on the part of the teachers federation on record, because some of the senior trustee associations might be watching and it might do the federation well suddenly to be faced with an irony such as that.
I did want to talk about the Time and Reader's Digest situation but I am not going to have the opportunity because time is pressing in. Time is always pressing in. However, I should like to say that I compliment two of the members on the Liberal side who spoke out against the bill. I know I was puzzled over the fact that this change in the 

budget was not handled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) but was brought in by the present Prime Minister. I understand that the Prime Minister was informed last week that several Canadian magazines have to fold within a few months unless they get some assurance that there will be legislation, and furthermore that the legislation will not give Reader's Digest and Time any special status.
The burden of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, tonight is directed toward the S.I.U. situation on the great lakes. This is a matter which has been very close to all of us. I think it was an emotional event for many of us last year when we voted to set up the trusteeship because it was inimical to the experience and attitudes of many of us. I should like to argue that the trustees adopted the wrong argument right from the start. Instead of taking the Norris commission report as their guide and following its recommendations, they decided to ignore it. They decided to make their own independent assessment of the situation and devise policies which they considered more suitable. The reason why they refused to abide by the advice of Justice Norris is obvious. Because his recommended procedures for creating democratic unionism on the great lakes would have been a long, difficult task, involving the trustees in years of ceaseless effort and toil, they chose the easy way. They looked at the situation and concluded that the cause of all the labour troubles was the existence of competing unions among the seamen. Put them all in one union, they thought, and there would be no longer any reason for that one union to stage boycotts or strikes, or harass shipping in any way.
Looking for the easy way out, they selected the S.I.U. as the best union to be given a monopoly over all sailors. Why? Because the
5.1.	U. already had the great majority of them, and it would be a lot simpler to assist the S.I.U. in gobbling up the rest than to try to get the smaller unions to replace the
5.1.	U. No matter that the S.I.U. was a jobselling racket; no matter that the inquiry of Mr. Justice Norris had exposed it as a hoodlum empire. It existed; it was the biggest organization; so it should be the one to represent all the seamen. Also, it had the big American stick of boycotts in American ports against a Canadian union.
The trustees, and apparently the federal government, were concerned only with restoring peace on the lakes. Peace at any price-peace at the price of surrendering to the very hoodlums that the Norris commission exposed that the trustees, at least according to my impression and that of my colleagues, were assigned to clean out. This is the kind of

peace the trustees have negotiated-a peace based on unconditional surrender to the S.I.U.
I think we know that the trustees have made a token effort to democratize the S.I.U., and I expect that some time next fall they will proclaim that the work of purification is complete; that free elections are being held, and that the S.I.U. is now worthy to be readmitted into the Canadian Labour Congress. But, no free election, no free referendum can be held while the enforcement machine of the S.I.U. remains intact along the waterfront.
The minister seems doubtful, even now, about the real tactics of the S.I.U. He seems to have difficulty in accepting that there is still a "do not ship" list. Well, they call it a registry of charges now. If the minister wants to find it I suggest he go to the fourth floor of the S.I.U. building in Montreal. Let him go to the north side of the room where he will find a robot filing system next to a large grey filing cabinet. That is where he will find the R.O.C. list which is, in effect, a "do not ship" list.
The trustees have apparently accepted Leonard J. "Red" McLaughlin as being a reformed character. As vice president of contract enforcement, McLaughlin was chief "enforcer" of the S.I.U.'s hoodlum empire in Canada. Mr. Justice Norris found that $72,000 out of $80,000 of Banks' "play money" in the brief period examined was not accounted for in any way. The remaining $8,000 was accounted for by meaningless chits- "$500 for information", "$1,000 for public relations", and so on. McLaughlin was in charge of the money. Yet Mr. Charles Millard says Mr. McLaughlin was a reliable servant of the union. Scores of sailors were brutally beaten in "jackal attacks" and many, such as Fred Neubauer, who had both his kneecaps broken by a crowbar, came forward to testify. These beaten sailors had one thing in common: they opposed the S.I.U. I would like to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and Mr. Charles Millard who they think paid out the money for these professional beatings? Why, the man who was in charge of the money, of course.
Leonard McLaughlin has been named- not charged, but named-along with Banks and an ex-S.I.U. Vancouver port agent, as co-conspirator in the formal charge against Banks for the beating, maiming and halfkilling of Richard Greaves, national president of the national association of marine engineers. Leonard McLaughlin was both the architect and the safe-keeper of the "do not ship" list, an infamous list now called the report of charges which contains the names of between 5,000 and 10,000 Canadian sailors.
The Budget-Mr. Fisher This vicious "do not ship" list is in effect at this moment in every S.I.U. hiring hall from Halifax to Vancouver, maintained by the maritime trustees in the name of the parliament of Canada. Every sailor who ever showed a spark of resistance to the Paul Hall-Hal Banks-Leonard McLaughlin hoodlum machine has his name on the "do not ship" list.
Mr. Justice Norris found McLaughlin to be a completely untrustworthy witness. He found McLaughlin responsible for the falsification of S.I.U. records. But the trustees now say he is a reformed man. McLaughlin was in charge of S.I.U. elections. The fraudulence of
S.I.U. elections was spelled out in detail before the Norris commission-more votes recorded for Banks, McLaughlin and the rest of the hoodlums than there were ballots cast. In a S.I.U. referendum a busy little group is described sitting around marking ballots by the bushel. But Mr. Charles Millard says McLaughlin is reformed. How naive is he? And how naive does he think we are? I wonder if the trustees have read about the role of Leonard McLaughlin and Paul Hall in the so-called Todd trial, described in great detail in the transcript of the Norris commission, in which Hall, Banks and McLaughlin turned a trial into a farce to destroy the protest movement against Banks' dictatorship. That was in 1952. I wonder if they have read of the role of McLaughlin at so-called conventions of the seafarers international union- conventions attended by only about 50 or 60 delegates-in support of one-man rule for Banks in Canada.
What an incredible defeat for the forces of decency in the Canadian labour movement is now unfolding before us. After a three year battle and a year long inquiry and report, the spoils, in the form of the clean unions, the exonerated unions-the national association of marine engineers, the Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers and the Canadian maritime union-are to be cut up and given to the criminals-the union found guilty-the seafarers international union. To this list I might add the Canadian merchant service guild-a clean if numerically weak body which the S.I.U. would have little trouble gobbling up in the future.
Why has this come about? It has come about because the trustees have let Paul Hall use his one club-control over the United States ports-to dictate terms of unconditional surrender. Instead of a spectacle of which we might be proud-Canadians demanding rights for Canadian ships and Canadian unions in American ports and threatening to close our ports if they do not open theirs- we have Paul Hall saying: If you want to sail into Chicago where my goons run the

The Budget-Mr. Fisher waterfront, you must (1) put my man McLaughlin in as president and (2) hand over the Canadian maritime union and the C.B.R.T. to me.
Well, the trustees have capitulated and the Minister of Labour defends them. And it is not just McLaughlin. Banks remains as vice president of the S.I.U. of North America, resident in Montreal-I ask hon. members to note that. The moment the trusteeship ends, McLaughlin again takes orders from Hal Banks. I want to know why the Canadian Labour Congress is silent about this. I want to know why Maurice Wright has not spoken up. He is the man who put together those extracts given to the Norris commission stating the C.L.C. position as to shipping on the great lakes. When one considers all the things the C.L.C. said before the Norris commission, why has it failed to respond at this new and crucial stage of the battle? Why does it appear to be making the very same mistake the Canadian labour movement, the T.L.C., made in 1948-49 when it helped to import the S.I.U. thugs in the first place? The answer to this question, I regret very much to say, is to be found in the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress is not yet fully able to act as a mature national labour centre in Canada, defending Canadian interests and expressing Canadian views. It is moving in the direction but it has not arrived yet at that point of development.
In a crisis between the Canadian and United States labour movements such as is involved here; with Paul Hall, a vice president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O.; with Hal Banks stronghly backed by George Meany, president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O.; with the powerful maritime trades department run by Paul Hall- in such a power struggle it would appear that the Canadian Labour Congress has to back down. I hope I am proven wrong. In the next few days, and especially at the C.L.C. convention which opens on April 20 in Montreal, the rank and file delegates, if not the leaders, can show me I am wrong and I hope they do. I hope we hear from Bill Dodge and Bill Smith about what I think is a sell-out by the national union in connection with a trusteeship such as this. If they fail to do this and the C.L.C. does not go on record in opposition to the continuation of the Paul Hall-Hal Banks-Red McLaughlin hoodlum empire and if they do not speak out for a Canadian resolution of the great lakes problem, rather than a solution dictated by American labour thugs, it will inevitably raise questions of a very fundamental kind about the relationship of any political party to the Canadian labour movement.
But what concerns us here in this house is something much more direct. We passed an act to establish a trusteeship to bring to an end the instruments of violence on the great lakes. The trustees instead have fallen prey to those whom they were commissioned to manage and control. Surely it is not possible for us to have continued confidence, on the basis of the facts as they are known to us, in these three misguided gentlemen, or in the bland assurances of an increasingly implausible Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen).
Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and
Commerce): Mr. Speaker, earlier today, in the course of what I think we will all agree was an inspiring contribution to this debate, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) called upon members of the house and upon Canadians generally to work for the strengthening of our confederation. I intend to begin my remarks this evening by referring to one aspect of this problem, trade and trade policy.
As Minister of Trade and Commerce my duties have taken me into every major area of this country and I have been impressed, as I have never been impressed before, by the diversity of Canada. It has been said by a distinguished historian that "Canada's existence does not and never has depended solely upon national uniformity. The Canadian confederation came into being not to crush but to reconcile regional diversities." I think one might go further and say that these regional diversities can survive and flourish only if they are reconciled in a thriving and united confederation.
These considerations, it seems to me, are just as relevant to the economic life of our country as to questions of language and culture. There must be room in the Canadian system for every region to achieve its true and full economic potential. There are bound to be variations from time to time, of course, in the rate of growth of different areas. However, as part of our nationhood we must see to it that no region is allowed to fall too far behind in economic development and living standards.
This is a responsibility that the federal and the provincial governments share together and must discharge in understanding and co-operation. Economic sectionalism may sometimes produce short term advantages for the sections of the country that indulge in it, but it is surely the road to economic weakness and retardation for the country as a whole and thus for its parts. Sectionalism of this kind is even more ill advised and self-defeating today than when it was rejected a century ago by the founders of this country. If Canada's industries are to compete with

those of the European economic community, the European free trade association and the United States they must be permitted to operate within our much smaller economy on the most rational and efficient basis possible. They must not be forced or induced by sectional economic policies to fragment their operations or produce in areas that are basically unsuitable for the type of industry concerned. Their products must receive fair and reasonable treatment throughout our country regardless of their centre of operations.
In his remarks the other day the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) referred to "steps recently taken by the Quebec government in banning the export of lumber", which he depicted as improper both legally and otherwise. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that his words reflect some misunderstanding which I think should be corrected. As I read it, the announcement made by the minister of mines and forests for the province of Quebec was to the effect that it was intended to enforce more strictly existing legislation concerning logs for lumber and veneering purposes taken from crown owned lands.
Apparently it is the intention of the province of Quebec now to enforce regulations which have been in effect for many years governing the use of logs taken from timber limits under lease from the crown in the right of the province. I see no constitutional question involved here. The lands under these timber leases are the property of the crown. The conditions under which the limits may be enjoyed by the leaseholders are matters of contract between the leaseholders and the crown. I believe it is correct that every province in Canada with major forest resources attaches important responsibilities to the use of logging timber leases whether for manufacture of lumber, plywood, pulp and paper or other forest products.
I might suggest to the hon. member for Peace River that he examine the statutes of his province affecting the conservation and use of natural resources, particularly oil and gas. I see no suggestion that what is intended in Quebec is "banning the export of lumber" as was stated by the hon. member. The government of Quebec is concerned with the supply of logs for manufacturing within the provinces as governed by conditions attached to the leases. As I think I have indicated previously to the house, I have had some informal conversations with members of the Quebec administration about this matter and the minister, Mr. Cliche, has recently made a statement on this point that I hope members of the house will find reassuring.
The Budget-Mr. Sharp
In making these remarks I do not wish to belittle the concern of the hon. member for Peace River. Like him, I am concerned about the question of barriers to trade and about economic sectionalism generally within Canada because I believe that freedom of trade between the provinces is of the utmost importance to the health of the Canadian economy. There is a heavy responsibility upon all of us, whether we are in provincial or federal governments or whether we are in our respective legislatures, to ensure that any intervention we make will strengthen and not weaken Canada. I can say for the federal government that we will discharge that responsibility.
I am hopeful that by building up the habit and practice of co-operation between federal and provincial authorities in the trade field we shall be able increasingly to reconcile divergent regional interests. At the conferences of federal and provincial trade ministers and officials during the past three months, which I and my officials called, we sought to find ways of working together more effectively in promoting Canada's external trade. While the federal government has the responsibility to take the leadership in this field, the provinces, we have recognized, also have a vital role to play.
Matters relating to external trade policy are, of course, the sole responsibility of the federal government. Canada must be able to speak with one voice at international trade conferences and negotiations and must be in a position to enter into international trade agreement commitments and to fulfil them. I should like to say to hon. members that this was acknowledged by all the provincial ministers without exception.
All of this brings me to make a few remarks about the forthcoming round of tariff and trade negotiations, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) invited me to do during this debate. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) referred to the prospect that these negotiations, known colloquially as the Kennedy round, would rank with the important trade negotiations that have taken place under the auspices of GATT since the end of the war. Hon. members may recall that the basis of these forthcoming negotiations was the decision of the GATT trade ministers last May when I attended the conference in Geneva on behalf of Canada. At that time several things were decided which I should perhaps recall: First, that the trade negotiations should begin on May 4, 1964; that the negotiations should be based on the principle of reciprocity; that there should be the widest possible participation in the negotiations; that

The Budget-Mr. Sharp the negotiations should cover all classes of products, whether industrial or agricultural; that the negotiations should deal with both tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade; that they should be based on a plan of substantially equal linear tariff cuts for certain of the more highly industrialized countries; that the trade negotiations should provide for acceptable conditions of access to world markets for agricultural products, and that every effort should be made to reduce barriers to exports of the less developed countries. It was on the basis of these principles as agreed to last May in Geneva that a trade negotiating committee was established to work out or negotiate a plan to supervise the conduct of the negotiations. This committee has been at work and it has been trying to work out the negotiating rules relating to the countries participating on a linear basis, and particularly the question of the depth of the tariff cut, and the way of dealing with this problem of tariff disparities.
Now, since these negotiating rules will have an important bearing on the results, one can say that the negotiations which we have been talking about as if they were to begin on May 4, have really already begun. These negotiations have, in fact, now been in progress for some months. Since this matter is of very considerable interest not only to the members of this house but to the community at large, I should like to deal briefly, and I hope clearly, with the problems that are now under discussion.
The essence of the problem of tariff disparities is to develop equitable rules for negotiations of equal linear tariff cuts between countries with differing tariff levels or structures. This problem, as hon. members may well recognize, arises particularly between the European economic community and the United States because the tariffs which now surround the European economic community are the result of an averaging process, a process which was necessary in order to make one community out of the six countries that entered into the European economic community. During this averaging process most of the tariff peaks were removed. The United States, on the other hand, has many low rates, but more particularly high rates in certain sectors, rates that are substantially above the rates of duty for the same items in the common market tariff. The six contend that where their tariff is significantly below the level of the comparable United States tariff an equal linear tariff cut would not yield an equivalence of benefit. Last May it was agreed that the trade negotiations committee should develop a criteria for determining where significant tariff disparities exist-that is disparities which are 
meaningful in trade terms-and to determine what special rules should be applicable for tariff reductions in such cases.
Since the likelihood is that where tariff disparities are found to exist there will be a smaller cut in tariffs, the question of the number of items accepted for special treatment has an important bearing on the total scope of the negotiations and on the question of reciprocity of benefit. It may also have an important bearing on the exceptions which would be made to the general rule, and particularly upon the general position of countries other than the United States and the European economic community, who will be affected by the depth of the tariff cuts made by them. Although progress has been made, the chief countries concerned have not yet resolved these difficult issues. Further meetings are scheduled between now and the opening date of May 4.
The second and perhaps most important point that was referred to the trade negotiating committee was the depth of the tariff cut. The United States trade legislation allows for cuts of up to 50 per cent on an across the board basis and with few exceptions. It also permits the removal of United States tariffs where the rates are 5 per cent or less. The discussions that have been going on in Geneva have been going forward on the working hypothesis of a 50 per cent cut. Whether this will become the actual rule for tariff reduction remains to be agreed. How much of the tariff of the United States, of the European economic community and of other countries will, in fact, be reduced in these negotiations cannot be finally known until the end of the negotiations. It will depend on the extent to which the participating countries are prepared to exchange meaningful concessions. The actual average incidence of the cut will be determined, not only by the general rate, whatever that may be, but also by the number of disparities involved and the number of exceptions made.
We for our part, and I am speaking now on behalf of Canada, are hoping that our trading partners will be prepared to go as far as possible in offering reductions to barriers to our export trade. There is every evidence to suggest that the United States administration is determined to offer maximum concessions to other countries within the scope of the authority received from congress. The United Kingdom and the continental E.F.T.A. countries have indicated that they intend to make substantial and positive response and they are interested, like the United States, in keeping exceptions to the minimum and narrowing the list of disparity items. The European economic community, on the other hand, has reaffirmed its support for a major

round of trade negotiations but attaches great importance to a satisfactory resolution, from its point of view, to the problem of tariff disparities and to other matters bearing on the scope and balance of the negotiations.
I have referred to exceptions. These are items which countries may consider it necessary to withhold from their linear offer. It was agreed by the minister last May that such exceptions should be kept to a bare minimum; that they should be subject in each case to confrontation and justification. The United States, by its own trade legislation, is required to exclude from its tariff offer lead and zinc and petroleum. Other countries do not have such legislative requirements. They may, however, be expected to come forward with certain items on which they do not feel able to offer tariff cuts. Such lists of exceptions and the scope of them might well become a key element in the negotiations themselves.
For example, it would clearly limit the value of the negotiations for Canada if items of particular interest in our trade were included in the exceptions lists of countries where we have important markets.
The working out of negotiating rules with respect to trade in agriculture is also proving to be both delicate and difficult. It is agreed that trade in agriculture should be an integral part of the negotiations and that the negotiations are to deal with the creation of acceptable conditions of access to world markets for agricultural products.
Here, however, special measures of protection as most hon. members know, designed to support farm economies by one means or another make it difficult, indeed well-nigh impossible, to apply the same negotiating rules to basic agricultural products as can be applied to the negotiations in the industrial sector. In many cases, some very important for Canada as an agricultural exporter, the tariff is not the effective barrier to trade. In other cases, the tariff is used in combination with other restrictive devices. None the less, for efficient agriculture producers whose international trade has a substantial agricultural content, meaningful negotiations on agriculture will be a critical element in a successful negotiation. This is so for Canada and for the United States as well as for Australia and New Zealand. The problem of finding a satisfactory negotiating base has had the added complexity that the European economic community is still in the process of formulating its common agricultural policy. It will require a good deal of imagination and good will to work out a solid settlement with the community in an area in which, for most basic agricultural products, the key element affecting production and therefore the scope
The Budget-Mr. Sharp for imports is the level of the support price, the system and the price being protected by a variable levy at the frontier which has the effect of bringing up the price of competitive imports to the level of prices prevailing in the domestic market.
While it is too early to be clear about the prospects in this sector, negotiations have been initiated for world cereals arrangements and there appears to be a readiness to bring agricultural supports and domestic production policies under international negotiation and confrontation. Meat groups and dairy products groups have been established to look into the possibility of special international arrangements for these products. Canada and other traditional exporters are placing the emphasis on access and satisfactory international prices. The Six tend to approach the question from the basis of acceptance of their agricultural system and a form of negotiation which would be related to it but which would emphasize the status quo rather than the expansion of competition between domestically produced and imported products.
I trust that between now and May 4 sufficient progress will have been made to permit us to see our way ahead in the agricultural sector as well as for industrial goods and materials.
I have dealt at some length with these matters because reports about them have, in some cases, tended to create uncertainties and doubts about the Kennedy round of negotiations itself. From what I have said I am sure the house will appreciate that the difficult and complex nature of the issues under discussion make it inevitable that progress will take time. Delays and problems should occasion neither surprise nor discouragement. The negotiations are scheduled to open in Geneva on May 4. A period of initial assessment will no doubt follow. By autumn we can expect the beginning of an extended period of intensive negotiations. It will, I think, be a year or more of negotiation before we reach the end of the road, and the road will not be smooth. Given effort and good will, the final results can, however, be substantial and worth while.
So far as our preparations here in Canada are concerned, hon. members will have seen the Prime Minister's announcement of February 21 appointing Mr. Norman Robertson, under secretary of state for external affairs, as Canada's chief negotiator, with responsibility to the government for Canada's participation in the negotiations. I think we are all grateful also that we have been able to get the services of Mr. Hector McKinnon, who is one of the most experienced negotiators in our service.

The Budget-Mr. Sharp
A tariffs and trade committee has been established, and has invited briefs from all Canadian interests concerned. There has already been a good response from Canadian interests, and briefs are coming in in volume. The Canadian business community is showing greater interest in these negotiations than in any previous negotiations, and I am certainly encouraged by the response we are receiving.
The committee is busy and the government is looking forward to having the benefit of its advice as the process of consultation, analysis and assessment goes forward. Later in the year a group will proceed to Geneva to negotiate in the Canadian interest, and we expect that through the actual negotiating stage necessary liaison with Canadian interests will be maintained through Ottawa.
Sometime during this debate reference was made to commonwealth trade. This was high on the agenda of the meeting of the commonwealth economic consultative committee I attended last May in London, on the eve of the GATT ministerial meeting, and at that time commonwealth ministers agreed on the continuing importance of commonwealth trade. They also agreed on the need for a general expansion of world trade and on the importance of this for all commonwealth countries.
Commonwealth countries generally have been playing an active role in the preparatory stages of the GATT trade negotiations. Whether they be developing countries, or chiefly agricultural exporters like New Zealand and Australia, or countries like Canada and the United Kingdom, each has made clear the important benefits for trade which they see possible through the Kennedy round, and there has been very strong support throughout the commonwealth for the forthcoming round of tariff negotiations.
As in the past, any major world trade negotiations involving substantial reductions in barriers to international trade will inevitably involve adjustments in the commonwealth preferences. To the extent, for example, that the United Kingdom reduces its most favoured nation rates, the margins of preference of commonwealth countries in access to the British market would be reduced. Similarly, a Canadian participation inevitably involves adjustments in preferences that, for example, the British are accorded in this market. While no detailed discussions have been held with the British government on this matter, we have been in touch and the two countries will be consulting closely throughout the negotiations with a view to ensuring that, whatever adjustments in the preferences may be necessary, they are worked out in consultation. Similarly, we

shall be in continuing close touch with the other commonwealth countries.
At the United Nations conference on trade and development, in which my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, participated, the question of extending new preferences and adjusting existing preferences is being actively studied as a possible means for assisting the less developed countries to improve their lot. It is important to understand that so far as our preferential arrangements with the less developed members of the commonwealth are concerned, criteria additional to considerations relating to Canada's trade directly with these countries will be brought to bear and may affect the future of these preferential arrangements.
Both my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I, have indicated to the house the sort of considerations that the government will be bearing in mind on this question of preferences.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to the position of state-trading countries in relation to these international negotiations. As hon. members are aware, Canada has found some important and valuable markets within the Sino-Soviet bloc. There is every reason to believe that this area will continue to have substantial food import requirements that we should be in a position to supply. The framework for these commercial exchanges has generally been worked out through bilateral negotiations in which I had some participation, and in which, I understand, one of the ministers of the former government had also. It has so far not been found possible to bring state-trading countries into a multilateral trading framework.
One of the challenges of the future, as market economies seek to develop closer commercial ties with socialist planned economy countries, will be to see whether a broad and more or less continuing framework of multilateral trade can be developed, in which state-trading countries and the needs of market economies can be fitted together on a mutually satisfactory basis.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, from the problems I have discussed how difficult and complex a situation faces both the GATT conference, and the United Nations conference now in progress. The finding of the way through them will require patience as well as diligence. We should expect what appear to be delays and set-backs from time to time. This is in the nature of important world trade negotiations. However, I am encouraged by the progress that is being made, and look forward to the launching of the Kennedy round on May 4 next, and to the serious and worth-while negotiations that lie ahead. In them Canada will seek to play its full part.

In so doing, the government believes that it is acting not only in the interests of the people of Canada but also of the people of the world at large.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to the less serious part of my speech I would like to make an announcement. The score, after one period of play at the Maple Leaf Gardens, is Toronto one Detroit one.

Now, Mr. Speaker, we heard a speech from the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in which he dealt in a very eloquent manner devoid of any partisan prejudice, with the problems facing the Canadian confederation.
The Prime Minister expressed some concern about the present situation. He went even so far as stating that the time for building up the Canadian nation was over, and that the challenge facing Canadians in 1964 was to save the Canadian nation, neither more nor less.
As far as I am concerned, I must say that those are feelings which certainly are to the credit of the Prime Minister, but when I heard him say so this afternoon, two things came to my mind which recently impressed me.
First of all, the too obvious inability of the government to turn those fine feelings into action. Second, in spite of the Prime Minister's obvious goodwill federal-provincial relations never were at such a low ebb.
As a member from the province of Quebec, I have-as all the other members in this house, I think-the progressive evolution of our Canadian confederation at heart. However, I cannot but repeat that, for Quebec and the whole of French Canada, confederation has always been considered as a pact between the two great founding races of this country. The document, which was by no means perfect, nevertheless made a splendid contribution to the development of a great country on this American soil.
If we look back at the last century of this country's history, we must admit that it has been a real success so far as human relations are concerned. Those who conceived it deserve all our gratitude. They knew how to reach a compromise when it was needed.
If we consider the situation as described by the Prime Minister this afternoon, we should not hesitate, we Canadians of 1964, to apply to present problems the same spirit of compromise which was so successful in 1867. By compromise, I mean the term defined by the late president John F. Kennedy in his remarkable book entitled "Profiles in
The Budget

Mr. Balcer Courage", that is the compromise to which politicians must resort in dealing with state matters.
Here is how the late President Kennedy defined the word compromise:

We shall need compromises in the days ahead to be sure, but these will be or should be compromises of issues, not of principles. We can compromise our political positions but not ourselves. We can resolve the clash of interest without conceding our ideals. And even the necessity for the right kind of compromise does not eliminate the need for those idealists and reformists who keep our compromises moving ahead. Compromise need not mean cowardice. Indeed it is frequently the compromisers and conciliators who are faced with the severest tests of political courage as they oppose the extremist views of their constituents.

I think that is a lesson in political history which applies to today's situation. And I do not hesitate for one second to call upon my compatriots and urge them to accept that definition in their relations with Canadian citizens in the rest of the country so that we can go hand in hand and build a great Canada for several more generations.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister specially dealt with the position of Quebec within the Canadian confederation. Since the last world war, great changes have happened in Canada, and especially in the province of Quebec. Quebec was swept by the great technological revolution which shook the free world in the fields of economy, social relations, education and national aspirations, because there is in Quebec a new vision.
The new generation has become conscious of the great opportunities which are opened to her in the field of technology and economy. Our youth is attracted by technical education. Our universities, our great schools of engineering, commerce and technology have doubled or tripled their enrolments.
Quebec was recently described by a reporter as a young giant waking up and becoming conscious of his strength; and I am convinced that all sincere Canadians are cheering at that surge of French Canadians. It is unavoidable that such a sudden awakening will create disturbances, but we must not let the initiative fall in the hands of extremists. On the other hand, we must not see separatism in every one of the least claims put forward by Quebec, nor talk about concessions every time Quebec wants her rights to be recognized.
This afternoon, the Prime Minister seemed to be seeking a way to prevent that division which may have occurred between the two major ethnical groups in Canada from getting any wider. He was looking for a means to strengthen national unity, a formula which

The Budget-Mr. Balcer would ensure for our country as brilliant a future as we seemed to have a few years ago.
I should like to suggest to my English speaking friends to imitate the example of Belgium and Switzerland and, in that connection, I call the attention of the house to a book written by a great journalist and a prominent member of the press gallery, Mrs. Ann Francis. That work, which was published by the Canadian institute of international affairs, is entitled: "Language-Bridge or Barrier".
Mrs. Francis wrote that booklet following a trip to Switzerland and Belgium. She described the situation existing in both countries and I believe the government could find there excellent solutions which could be applied to today's problems.
Let us remember that we have the example of Belgium where centralization has caused the dispute between Flemish and Walloon; so much so that today the country is divided and bloody riots break out at regular intervals. On the other hand, we have the example of Switzerland where minorities are treated intelligently and where the majority has established an atmosphere of peace, prosperity and mutual confidence, which has allowed Switzerland to develop and become a country respected everywhere in the world.
Let me quote the words of the minister of external affairs of Switzerland when asked by Mrs. Francis about his secret to remedy the situation and give satisfaction to the minorities, the minister had this answer:
"We have had our troubles. It took us many years to find the answer. Quite simply it is this. We spoil them".
Dr. Hans Zbinden, a leading sociologist at the University of Berne, said to Mrs. Francis:

"We must not only respect minorities. We must make them feel we love them for their diversity".

Mrs. Francis added the following:

These are not merely beautiful theories to impress a stranger. According to Dr. Hermann Weilen-mann, a foremost Swiss historian:
"Although fewer than 30 per cent of the population speak romance languages, they are represented in the federal cabinet by three out of seven councillors. In the same way, there is a tendency to give linguistic, regional and often religious, minorities proportionally more voice on commissions and in the departments of the federal government and the cantons than their numbers would warrant. Likewise minorities are often given more subsidies than the majority to make them take a greater interest in communal affairs".
These might seem to be quite strong arguments in favour of greater advantages for minorities in Canada.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that they must be quite serious after all, especially when they face such a situation over there, and that we should find among these various suggestions a formula that could be applied to Canada and which would solve our linguistic problems.
This afternoon, the Prime Minister expressed his deep concern over the situation facing us. His voice was not as depressed as when he made his statement on the results of the last federal-provincial conference, but I think that we understand his concern and we are in sympathy with him.
His government is on the verge of getting blamed, in Quebec, for double taxation which will no doubt result from the way Quebec was treated at that federal-provincial conference. His government is once again forced to withdraw its pension plan because it was obviously ill-prepared and it was too anxious, for some unknown reason, to impose its point of view on the provinces.
As far as the Conservative party is concerned, we are in favour of a national pension fund, but we want a plan which will respect the rights of the provinces in that field and will enable all Canadians to enjoy a well-deserved, comfortable and dignified retirement.
Mr. Speaker, we are at the crossroads in Canada, and I am of the opinion that all hon. members should make every effort to bring about the best understanding possible between all groups in the country. As for us, Conservatives, we have a long tradition of fostering mutual respect between Canadians and we wish to assure the house that we will fully support any measure designed to strengthen the bonds which unite the two great founding races of our country.
I wish to remind you that we must give evidence of tolerance and mutual respect because we are responsible for the future of a great country. I am convinced that we will not elude this challenge and that every one of us will do his duty. On the other hand, I hope the government will pull itself together, be better prepared and introduce a truly serious policy, carefully thought-out pieces of legislation that the house could really support unanimously.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that this is rather a late hour to be participating in a debate such as this, but nevertheless I appreciate the opportunity of making a few observations with respect to the issues before us. We have dealt down through the course of this debate with a great variety of subjects. There are those
